segments.voiceover: Welcome to part two of our white blood cell review. Today we'll explore the essential pathology and clinical reasoning you need to master for your board exam.

This lecture covers white blood cell neoplasms. We'll start with general diagnostic approaches including cell surface markers, cytogenetics, and prognostic factors. Then we'll explore B cell neoplasms including Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B cell lymphoma, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. We'll also cover T cell neoplasms, plasma cell dyscrasias, and miscellaneous conditions.

This table is your one-stop cheat sheet for B-cell lymphoma translocations, and examiners love it because almost every partner is the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, IGH, sitting at 14q32. So when you see the number fourteen and q32, think IGH driving overexpression of whatever oncogene it grabs. Start at the top: the t 8;14 translocation puts MYC under IGH control, and that's Burkitt lymphoma in over ninety-eight percent, though MYC can also show up in DLBCL, follicular, and myeloma. Next, t 3;14 activates B C L 6, classically DLBCL. The one they hammer most is t 14;18, IGH-BCL2, follicular lymphoma in about eighty percent, and roughly twenty percent of DLBCL. Then t 11;14, IGH-cyclin D1, is mantle cell in over ninety-five percent, and also myeloma in about twenty to twenty-five percent. For the MALT lymphomas, know two: t 1;14 driving B C L 10, and the t 11;18 BIRC3-MALT1 fusion, which notably does NOT involve IGH and predicts resistance to H. pylori eradication. Finally t 6;14 activates IRF4 in about twenty percent of myeloma.

keypoints: t(8;14) → MYC = Burkitt (>98%); also DLBCL, FL, myeloma
t(11;14) → CCND1/cyclin D1 = MCL (>95%), myeloma 20-25%
MALToma: t(1;14) BCL10 & t(11;18) BIRC3::MALT1 fusion
t(3;14)→BCL6 (DLBCL); t(6;14)→IRF4 (myeloma ~20%); most partner IGH at 14q32
segments.voiceover: Lock in the big four. The t 8;14 translocation means MYC and Burkitt, over ninety-eight percent. t 14;18 is BCL2 and follicular lymphoma, about eighty percent. t 11;14 is cyclin D1 and mantle cell, over ninety-five percent, plus some myeloma. For MALT lymphoma, remember t 1;14 with B C L 10 and the t 11;18 BIRC3-MALT1 fusion. And note that most partners join IGH at 14q32.

This table is the T-cell counterpart to the B-cell cytogenetics slide, and the theme is the same: most of these translocations juxtapose an oncogene to a T-cell receptor locus, driving overexpression. Notice the pattern in the products column. The T-cell receptor genes are the partners, T R B on chromosome 7, T R A and T R D on chromosome 14. So when you see a breakpoint at 7 q 34 or 14 q 11, think T-cell receptor. The top rows are all T-lymphoblastic lymphoma, and the high-yield associations are the oncogenes each partner activates. The t 7;7 or inversion 7 drives HOXA cluster overexpression. The t 1;14 or t 1;7 drives TAL1, the single most classic oncogene in T-cell A L L. The t 7;9 activates NOTCH1, the master regulator of T-cell fate. The t 8;14 drives MYC, and the t 5;14 drives T L X 3. The individual frequencies are low, roughly three to five percent at most, so don't over-memorize the exact percents. The two rows examiners actually reward are at the bottom. The t 8;13 gives an FGFR2, ZMYM2 fusion tied to a myeloproliferative neoplasm associated with T-lymphoblastic lymphoma. And the money answer, the t 2;5, produces the A L K, N P M 1 fusion of anaplastic large cell lymphoma, accounting for about eighty-four percent of A L K-positive cases.

keypoints: T-cell partners = TCR loci: TRB (7q34), TRA/TRD (14q11)
t(1;14)/t(1;7) → TAL1; t(7;9) → NOTCH1 — classic T-ALL/T-LBL oncogenes
t(2;5)(p23;q35) → ALK::NPM1 = ALCL (~84% of ALK+ cases)
t(8;13) → FGFR2::ZMYM2 = MPN associated with T-LBL
segments.voiceover: Key points to lock in. The T-cell partner is almost always a T-cell receptor locus, T R B at 7 q 34 or T R A and T R D at 14 q 11. The t 1;14 and t 1;7 drive TAL1, and the t 7;9 drives NOTCH1, the classic T-lymphoblastic oncogenes. The one they love most, the t 2;5, gives the A L K, N P M 1 fusion of anaplastic large cell lymphoma, about eighty-four percent of A L K-positive cases. The t 8;13 gives an FGFR2, ZMYM2 fusion linked to a myeloproliferative neoplasm with T-L B L. And remember MYC from t 8;14 and T L X 3 from t 5;14.

This slide is a classic board matching exercise: connect each lymphoid malignancy to its prognostic and staging system. Start with the universals. Lugano is your general anatomic staging system for lymphoma, and Lugano also defines treatment response criteria, while I-M-W-G response criteria belong to myeloma. Now go disease by disease. For diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, know cell-of-origin, germinal center versus non-germinal center, assigned by the Hans algorithm on immunohistochemistry, plus the International Prognostic Index and its variants: revised I-P-I, N-C-C-N I-P-I, and the C-N-S I-P-I that predicts central nervous system relapse. Follicular lymphoma pairs with FLIPI and FLIPI-2, and the GELF criteria define high tumor burden, meaning who needs treatment versus watchful waiting. Mantle cell lymphoma is MIPI. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is prognosticated by cytogenetics, TP53, and IGHV mutation status, but staged clinically by Rai and Binet. Hodgkin lymphoma uses the International Prognostic Score. Waldenstrom uses the ISS for Waldenstrom, ISSWM. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma uses I-P-I, the PIT, and the T-cell score. And myeloma is risk-stratified by cytogenetics and staged by the ISS, revised ISS, and the newer R-2-ISS.

keypoints: General: Lugano staging + response; IMWG = myeloma response
DLBCL: Hans algorithm (GCB/non-GCB), IPI/R-IPI/NCCN-IPI/CNS-IPI
FL: FLIPI, FLIPI-2; GELF = tumor burden/when to treat. MCL: MIPI
CLL: del/TP53/IGHV prognosis; Rai & Binet staging. HL: IPS
WM: ISSWM. PTCL: IPI/PIT/T-cell score. Myeloma: ISS/R-ISS/R2-ISS + cytogenetics
segments.voiceover: Key associations to lock in: Lugano for general staging and response, I-M-W-G for myeloma response. DLBCL, use the Hans algorithm and the I-P-I family, including C-N-S I-P-I. Follicular is FLIPI, with GELF telling you when to treat. Mantle cell is MIPI. C-L-L uses TP53 and IGHV for prognosis but Rai and Binet for staging. Hodgkin is I-P-S, Waldenstrom is ISSWM, T-cell lymphoma is I-P-I, PIT, and T-cell score, and myeloma is the ISS series.

Now let's turn to Hodgkin lymphoma. It's unique among lymphoid neoplasms because the malignant cells are rare and buried in a reactive background, and its classification, immunophenotype, staging, and treatment algorithms are all high-yield board topics we'll walk through next.

This slide lays out the modern classification of Hodgkin lymphoma and the immunophenotype that separates its two major forms. Under WHO-HAEM5, Hodgkin lymphoma splits into nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma and classical Hodgkin lymphoma, and classical Hodgkin lymphoma has four subtypes you should be able to rattle off: nodular sclerosis, lymphocyte-rich, mixed cellularity, and lymphocyte-depleted. Now here's the twist the slide is flagging: the 2022 International Consensus Classification, the ICC, renamed nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma to nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma, essentially demoting it out of the Hodgkin family because biologically it behaves like a B-cell lymphoma. The immunophenotype proves the point. The neoplastic cell in that entity is the LP cell, the popcorn cell, and it's CD3 negative, CD20 positive, CD45 positive, CD79a positive, CD15 negative, CD30 negative, PAX-5 positive, and BCL6 positive, essentially a normal B-cell marker profile. Contrast that with the Reed-Sternberg cell of classical Hodgkin lymphoma, which is CD3 negative, CD20 negative, CD45 negative, CD79a negative, but flips to CD15 positive, CD30 positive, with only weak PAX-5. That CD15 and CD30 positive, CD45 and CD20 negative pattern is the single most tested immunophenotype in Hodgkin lymphoma.

keypoints: WHO-HAEM5: NLPHL vs classical HL (nodular sclerosis, lymphocyte-rich, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-depleted)
ICC 2022 renamed NLPHL to nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma
LP/popcorn cell: CD20+/CD79a+/PAX-5+/BCL6+, CD15-/CD30-/CD45+
RS cell (classical HL): CD15+/CD30+, CD20-/CD45-/CD79a-, PAX-5 weak
High-yield: CD15+/CD30+ but CD45- and CD20- = classical HL signature
segments.voiceover: Lock in two immunophenotypes. The LP or popcorn cell of nodular lymphocyte predominant disease is CD20 positive, CD79a positive, CD15 negative, CD30 negative, essentially a B-cell profile, which is why the ICC 2022 stripped the Hodgkin label and renamed it nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma. The Reed-Sternberg cell of classical Hodgkin lymphoma flips that: CD15 positive, CD30 positive, but CD45 negative, CD20 negative, and only weak PAX-5. That contrast is exam gold.

This slide covers Hodgkin lymphoma prognostic factors, and it splits cleanly into early stage versus advanced stage systems, which boards love to test separately. For early stage, meaning stage I to II disease, three cooperative groups, the German Hodgkin Study Group, the EORTC, and the NCCN, each define unfavorable risk factors that determine whether a patient gets combined modality therapy versus chemotherapy alone. The factors overlap heavily: elevated ESR combined with B symptoms, a large mediastinal mass measured as a mediastinal mass ratio greater than about a third, more than two or three involved nodal sites depending on the group, extranodal extension called an E lesion, and bulky disease generally over ten centimeters. You don't need to memorize every cutoff by group, but you should recognize the categories: age, ESR plus B symptoms, mediastinal bulk, nodal sites, and E lesions. For advanced stage disease, the tool is the International Prognostic Score, the IPS, which assigns one point per adverse factor, seven factors total, and is remembered with the mnemonic A2S2L2H: albumin under 4, age over 45, stage IV disease, male sex, leukocytosis over 15,000, lymphocytopenia under 600 or under 8 percent of the white count, and hemoglobin under 10.5. Higher IPS scores correlate with worse progression-free and overall survival and increasingly guide treatment intensification.

keypoints: Early stage (I-II): GHSG, EORTC, NCCN unfavorable risk factors
Unfavorable factors: high ESR + B symptoms, bulky mediastinal mass, >2-3 nodal sites, E lesion
Advanced stage: International Prognostic Score (IPS), 1 point per factor, 7 factors
Mnemonic A2S2L2H: Albumin<4, Age>45, Stage IV, Sex male, Leukocytosis>15K, Lymphocytopenia, Hgb<10.5
segments.voiceover: Two systems to separate clearly. Early stage one and two disease uses unfavorable risk factors from GHSG, EORTC, and NCCN: think high ESR with B symptoms, bulky mediastinal mass, and multiple nodal sites. Advanced stage disease uses the International Prognostic Score, one point each for seven factors, best remembered as A2S2L2H: albumin under 4, age over 45, stage IV, sex male, leukocytosis over 15,000, lymphocytopenia, and hemoglobin under 10.5.

This slide walks through how we actually treat classical Hodgkin lymphoma, and the key concept is that therapy is both risk-adjusted and response-adapted. Risk-adjusted means we ask up front whether disease is unfavorable or bulky, which sets the starting regimen. Response-adapted means we use interim FDG-PET imaging mid-treatment to escalate or de-escalate therapy, and the pivotal trial here is RATHL, response-adapted therapy in Hodgkin lymphoma. In RATHL, over 1200 newly diagnosed patients got two cycles of ABVD, then an interim PET scan. PET-negative patients continued on ABVD or dropped the bleomycin to AVD, while PET-positive patients escalated to intensified BEACOPP. Three-year progression-free survival was 85 percent with ABVD or AVD versus 68 percent with escalated BEACOPP in the PET-positive group, which tells you PET positivity itself is a marker of higher-risk biology. By stage and risk group: favorable stage I-II gets three cycles of ABVD; unfavorable non-bulky stage I-II gets two cycles of ABVD followed by four of AVD; unfavorable bulky stage I-II adds involved-site radiotherapy, ISRT, after the same chemo backbone. Advanced stage III-IV historically got six cycles of ABVD plus ISRT, but the modern NCCN preferred regimens have shifted toward novel combinations: nivolumab-AVD, BrECADD, and brentuximab vedotin-AVD, all built to reduce bleomycin-related pulmonary toxicity while improving outcomes.

keypoints: Risk-adjusted (unfavorable/bulky) + response-adapted (interim PET) treatment
RATHL: ABVD x2 -> PET; PET- continue ABVD/AVD, PET+ escalate to BEACOPP
RATHL 3-yr PFS: 85% (ABVD/AVD) vs 68% (escalated BEACOPP arm)
Stage I-II: ABVD(3) favorable; ABVD/AVD +/- ISRT if unfavorable/bulky
Stage III-IV: newer options replacing bleomycin - Nivo-AVD, BrECADD, BV-AVD
segments.voiceover: Two concepts drive Hodgkin treatment: risk-adjusted therapy based on unfavorable or bulky features at diagnosis, and response-adapted therapy guided by interim PET, as shown in the RATHL trial, where PET-negative patients stayed on ABVD or AVD with 85 percent 3-year PFS, while PET-positive patients needed escalated BEACOPP. For advanced stage III and IV disease, remember the newer bleomycin-sparing regimens replacing classic ABVD: nivolumab-AVD, BrECADD, and brentuximab vedotin-AVD.

This slide is the pivotal ECHELON-1 trial data, the trial that established brentuximab vedotin plus AVD, written as A plus AVD, as a frontline option for advanced stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma. The design compared A plus AVD against standard ABVD in previously untreated stage III to IV patients. The primary endpoint was modified progression-free survival, meaning progression, death, or the need for subsequent anti-cancer therapy after an incomplete response. The trial met that endpoint: two-year modified PFS was 82.1 percent with A plus AVD versus 77.2 percent with ABVD, a hazard ratio of 0.77, statistically significant with a log-rank p-value of 0.04. Framed differently, that's a 23 percent reduction in the risk of a PFS event with A plus AVD compared with ABVD by independent review. Looking at the reasons for events, disease progression was the dominant driver in both arms, 90 events with A plus AVD versus 102 with ABVD, but incomplete response requiring subsequent therapy was notably lower with A plus AVD, 9 versus 22 patients. The key takeaway for boards: ECHELON-1 is the trial, published by Connors and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018, that swapped bleomycin for brentuximab vedotin in the AVD backbone and showed a survival benefit, setting up the bleomycin-sparing regimens we see as NCCN preferred options today.

keypoints: ECHELON-1: brentuximab vedotin + AVD (A+AVD) vs ABVD, advanced-stage HL
Primary endpoint (modified PFS) met: HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.60-0.98), p=0.04
2-yr modified PFS: A+AVD 82.1% vs ABVD 77.2%
23% reduction in risk of PFS event with A+AVD vs ABVD
Connors JM et al, NEJM 2018;378:331-44
segments.voiceover: ECHELON-1 is a must-know trial: brentuximab vedotin plus AVD versus standard ABVD in advanced Hodgkin lymphoma. The primary endpoint, modified progression-free survival, was met, with a hazard ratio of 0.77 and a 23 percent risk reduction favoring A plus AVD, at 82.1 percent versus 77.2 percent two-year modified PFS. This is the trial that justified replacing bleomycin with brentuximab vedotin in frontline therapy.

This slide stacks three trials together to show the evolution of frontline regimens for advanced Hodgkin lymphoma, and it's worth tracing the sequence. On the left is BrECADD, a PET-adapted regimen combining brentuximab vedotin with etoposide, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, dacarbazine, and dexamethasone, tested here specifically in older patients, ages 61 to 75, a population that tolerates standard intensified regimens poorly. With interim PET-guided cycle number, two-year progression-free survival was 91.5 percent and 82 percent achieved complete response, published in the Lancet in 2024, showing this de-escalated, biomarker-guided approach works even in an older, more fragile population. On the right are two head-to-head comparisons that map the modern treatment ladder. First, brentuximab vedotin plus AVD beat standard ABVD, that's the ECHELON-1 result we just covered, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022. Then, nivolumab plus AVD was compared against brentuximab vedotin plus AVD in a large study of nearly a thousand patients with stage III or IV classical Hodgkin lymphoma, and at the second interim analysis, nivolumab-AVD significantly improved progression-free survival, hazard ratio 0.48, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2024. Notably, nivolumab was also better tolerated, with only 9.4 percent discontinuing treatment versus 22.2 percent on brentuximab vedotin. So the ladder is ABVD, then brentuximab vedotin-AVD beats ABVD, then nivolumab-AVD beats brentuximab vedotin-AVD, reflecting the field's steady move toward checkpoint inhibitor-based frontline therapy.

keypoints: BrECADD (elderly, PET-adapted): 2-yr PFS 91.5%, 82% CR - Lancet 2024
ECHELON-1: BV+AVD > ABVD - NEJM 2022;387:310-320
SWOG S1826: Nivo-AVD > BV+AVD, HR 0.48, stage III/IV cHL - NEJM 2024;391:1379
Nivo-AVD better tolerated: 9.4% discontinuation vs 22.2% with BV-AVD
Treatment evolution ladder: ABVD -> BV+AVD -> Nivo-AVD
segments.voiceover: Trace the frontline treatment ladder for advanced classical Hodgkin lymphoma: brentuximab vedotin plus AVD beat ABVD in ECHELON-1, then nivolumab plus AVD beat brentuximab vedotin plus AVD in the SWOG S1826 trial, with a hazard ratio of 0.48 and fewer discontinuations. And for older, less fit patients, BrECADD with PET-adapted dosing achieved a 91.5 percent two-year progression-free survival.

This slide zeroes in on nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, and the title itself makes the key point: as of the 2022 International Consensus Classification, it's no longer classified as Hodgkin lymphoma at all, it's renamed nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma. The neoplastic cells are lymphocyte predominant cells, nicknamed popcorn cells for their multilobulated nuclei, and they're CD20 positive, CD79a positive, BCL6 positive, but CD15 negative and CD30 negative, a phenotype that looks like a germinal center B-cell rather than a classical Reed-Sternberg cell. Biologically, this entity may sit at one end of a spectrum whose other end is T-cell and histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma, THRLBCL, since both share a B-cell-derived neoplastic clone sitting in a reactive T-cell and histiocyte background, just with different growth patterns. The clinical behavior is generally favorable: an indolent course with good overall prognosis, though patients can have occasional late relapses even a decade out, which the survival curve on this slide illustrates nicely compared to classical Hodgkin lymphoma. About 3 to 5 percent of cases progress to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma over time, which matters for surveillance. And because these are CD20 positive B-cell tumors, not classical Hodgkin, treatment shifts toward rituximab-based systemic regimens: R-AVBD, R-CHOP, or R-CVP, rather than the ABVD-based approach used for classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

keypoints: ICC 2022: NLPHL renamed nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma (NLPBCL)
LP/popcorn cells: CD20+/CD79a+/BCL6+, CD15-/CD30- (B-cell phenotype, not classical HL)
Spectrum with THRLBCL (T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma)
3-5% progress to DLBCL; indolent course but occasional late relapse
Treatment: rituximab-based - R-ABVD, R-CHOP, R-CVP (CD20+ drives anti-CD20 therapy)
segments.voiceover: Remember that NLPHL was reclassified by the ICC in 2022 as nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma, dropping the Hodgkin label because the LP or popcorn cells are CD20 positive, CD79a positive, BCL6 positive, and CD15 and CD30 negative, a true B-cell phenotype. It sits on a spectrum with T-cell and histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma, three to five percent progress to DLBCL, and because it's CD20 positive, treatment is rituximab-based: R-ABVD, R-CHOP, or R-CVP.

This slide covers AETHERA, the pivotal trial establishing brentuximab vedotin maintenance after autologous stem cell transplant in high-risk Hodgkin lymphoma. Think through the eligibility logic first: patients enter after frontline therapy, get restaged, and are flagged as high risk if they were refractory to frontline treatment, relapsed within 12 months of frontline therapy, or relapsed at 12 months or later but with extranodal involvement. Those high-risk patients get salvage therapy, restaging, and if they achieve complete response, partial response, or stable disease, they proceed to autologous stem cell transplant. Thirty to 45 days after transplant, this phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomized them to brentuximab vedotin maintenance versus placebo. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival by independent review, with overall survival and safety as secondary endpoints. The results were striking: median PFS was not reached in the brentuximab vedotin arm, with a 5-year PFS of 59 percent, compared to a median PFS of only 15.8 months and a 5-year PFS of 41 percent with placebo, an overall 48 percent reduction in risk of progression or death, hazard ratio 0.521. The takeaway for boards: post-transplant consolidation with brentuximab vedotin is now standard of care for Hodgkin patients with these specific high-risk features, and this is the trial that proves it.

keypoints: AETHERA: phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled - BV maintenance post-ASCT
High-risk criteria: refractory to frontline, relapse <12mo, or relapse >=12mo with extranodal disease
Primary endpoint: PFS per IRF; BV mPFS not reached (5-yr PFS 59%) vs placebo mPFS 15.8mo (5-yr PFS 41%)
48% reduction in risk of progression/death with BV, HR 0.521 (0.379-0.717)
segments.voiceover: AETHERA established brentuximab vedotin as post-transplant maintenance in high-risk Hodgkin lymphoma, meaning patients refractory to frontline therapy, relapsed within 12 months, or relapsed later with extranodal disease. Median PFS was not reached with brentuximab vedotin, 5-year PFS 59 percent, versus 15.8 months and 41 percent with placebo, a 48 percent reduction in risk, hazard ratio 0.521. This is now standard post-ASCT consolidation for high-risk patients.

This is the pivotal trial behind brentuximab vedotin in relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma. S-G-zero-three-five, dash, zero-zero-zero-three was an international, single-arm, phase two study that enrolled one hundred two heavily pretreated patients whose Hodgkin lymphoma had relapsed or failed after high dose therapy and autologous stem cell transplant. Patients needed F-D-G avid disease on PET and good performance status. They received brentuximab vedotin, one point eight milligrams per kilogram every three weeks, for up to sixteen cycles, with response assessed by an independent review facility using interim PET scans and serial CT imaging. The primary endpoint was overall response rate, with duration of response, complete response rate, progression free survival, overall survival, and safety as key secondary endpoints. The results were impressive: overall response rate of seventy five percent, complete response in thirty four percent with median duration not yet reached, and ninety four percent of patients showing some tumor shrinkage. Median progression free survival was five point six months, but patients achieving complete response had a median duration of response of twenty point five months. This trial established brentuximab vedotin as standard initial salvage therapy for relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma after autologous transplant failure.

keypoints: Phase 2, single-arm trial: BV 1.8 mg/kg Q3W, up to 16 cycles, R/R HL post-ASCT (N=102)
Primary endpoint ORR; key secondary DOR, CR rate, PFS, OS, safety
ORR 75%, CR rate 34%, median DOR not reached
PFS 5.6 months; median DOR in CR patients 20.5 months
Established BV as standard therapy for post-transplant relapsed HL
segments.voiceover: Remember this as the trial that defined brentuximab vedotin's role after autologous transplant failure in Hodgkin lymphoma. Single-arm phase two, one hundred two patients, B-V at standard dosing for up to sixteen cycles. Overall response rate seventy five percent, complete response thirty four percent, and a striking twenty point five month median duration of response in those who achieved complete remission. This is the data set that earned B-V its label for post-A-S-C-T relapse.

This slide covers the checkpoint inhibitor data in relapsed refractory Hodgkin lymphoma. The biologic rationale is genetic: classical Hodgkin lymphoma frequently carries amplification of chromosome nine, p, twenty four, which co-amplifies the PD-1 ligand genes and JAK2. Increased JAK2 signaling further upregulates PD-1 ligand expression, driving both immune evasion and increased proliferation of the malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells, which is why PD-1 blockade works so well in this disease. Nivolumab, studied in patients who had failed both autologous transplant and brentuximab vedotin, achieved an overall response rate of sixty six point three percent. The most common grade three to four adverse events were neutropenia and lipase elevation, each around five percent, with pyrexia being the most common severe adverse event; nivolumab received F-D-A approval on this basis. Pembrolizumab, studied in the KEYNOTE-zero-eight-seven trial in the same relapsed refractory population, achieved a similar overall response rate of sixty nine percent, with fatigue as the main adverse event, and was likewise F-D-A approved. Together these trials made PD-1 inhibitors a standard option for Hodgkin lymphoma relapsing after transplant and brentuximab.

keypoints: 9p24 amplification co-amplifies PD-1 ligand genes and JAK2, driving immune evasion and proliferation
Nivolumab: ORR 66.3% in post-ASCT, post-BV relapsed HL; grade 3-4 neutropenia and lipase rise (~5% each); FDA approved
Pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-087): ORR 69%, mainly fatigue; FDA approved
Both PD-1 inhibitors are standard salvage after ASCT and brentuximab vedotin failure
segments.voiceover: The key biology is nine p twenty four amplification, which co-amplifies PD-1 ligand and JAK2, giving Hodgkin Reed-Sternberg cells a built-in immune escape mechanism, and that is exactly why PD-1 blockade works so well here. Nivolumab and pembrolizumab both showed response rates in the mid to high sixty percent range in patients who had already failed autologous transplant and brentuximab vedotin, and both are F-D-A approved in that setting. Know the toxicity signatures: neutropenia and lipase elevation for nivolumab, fatigue for pembrolizumab.

We now shift gears to diffuse large B cell lymphoma, or D-L-B-C-L, the most common aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma. In this section we will work through the prognostic scoring systems, the Hans algorithm for cell of origin classification, and the double hit versus double expresser distinction, all of which show up repeatedly on boards.

This is the International Prognostic Index, or I-P-I, and its revised version, R-I-P-I, for diffuse large B cell lymphoma. The original I-P-I scores five clinical factors, one point each: age over sixty, Ann Arbor stage three or four, E-C-O-G performance status two or higher, elevated serum L-D-H above the upper limit of normal, and more than one extranodal site of disease. Total points define four risk groups: low, zero to one point; low-intermediate, two points; high-intermediate, three points; and high, four to five points. But this original I-P-I was derived in the pre-rituximab era, so it was recalibrated after rituximab became standard, producing the revised I-P-I, which regroups the same five factors into just three categories: very good, zero points; good, one to two points; and poor, three to five points. The Kaplan-Meier curves show excellent discrimination: four year progression free survival is ninety four percent for very good, eighty percent for good, and fifty three percent for poor, with a similar pattern for four year overall survival, ninety four, seventy nine, and fifty five percent respectively.

keypoints: IPI: 1 point each for age >60, stage III/IV, ECOG ≥2, LDH >ULN, >1 extranodal site
IPI groups (pre-rituximab): low 0-1, low-intermediate 2, high-intermediate 3, high 4-5
R-IPI (rituximab era) regroups same factors: very good 0, good 1-2, poor 3-5
4-year PFS/OS: very good 94%/94%, good 80%/79%, poor 53%/55%
segments.voiceover: Know the five I-P-I factors cold: age over sixty, advanced stage, poor performance status, high L-D-H, and multiple extranodal sites, one point each. The original I-P-I splits into four risk groups, but since it predates rituximab, boards favor the revised I-P-I, which condenses those same factors into three groups, very good, good, and poor, with four year survival ranging from about ninety four percent down to around fifty five percent.

The N-C-C-N I-P-I is a refinement of the original index designed to better separate outcomes at the extremes of risk. Instead of binary cutoffs, age is now scored in four tiers: zero points for forty or younger, one point for forty one to sixty, two points for sixty one to seventy five, and three points for over seventy five. Serum L-D-H is similarly scored in three tiers based on the ratio to the upper limit of normal, up to three points. E-C-O-G performance status and Ann Arbor stage are scored as before, zero or one point. Extranodal disease is redefined more specifically as involvement of bone marrow, central nervous system, liver, gastrointestinal tract, or lung, rather than simply counting sites. Total scores define four groups: low, zero to one; low-intermediate, two to three; high-intermediate, four to five; and high, six or more. The survival curves from the original validation cohort show much wider separation between these four groups than the classic I-P-I achieved, particularly better identifying the truly low risk and truly high risk patients.

keypoints: Age scored in 4 tiers (≤40, 41-60, 61-75, >75); LDH ratio scored in 3 tiers (up to 3 points)
Extranodal sites redefined as major organ involvement: bone marrow, CNS, liver, GI, or lung
ECOG and Ann Arbor stage still scored 0 or 1 point as in classic IPI
4 risk groups: low 0-1, low-intermediate 2-3, high-intermediate 4-5, high ≥6
Better separates outcomes at the low- and high-risk extremes than the original IPI
segments.voiceover: The N-C-C-N I-P-I refines the classic index by weighting age and L-D-H more granularly and by restricting extranodal disease to specific major organs, bone marrow, C-N-S, liver, G-I tract, and lung. This produces four risk groups, low through high, and it discriminates outcomes at the risk extremes better than the original I-P-I, which is why it is increasingly favored in modern practice.

The C-N-S I-P-I predicts risk of central nervous system relapse in diffuse large B cell lymphoma, which is a distinct and clinically important question from general prognosis. It uses the same five classic I-P-I factors, age over sixty, advanced Ann Arbor stage, E-C-O-G performance status two or higher, elevated L-D-H, and more than one extranodal site, each worth one point, and adds a sixth factor: kidney or adrenal gland involvement, also one point. Total score defines three risk groups: low, zero to one point; intermediate, two to three points; and high, four to six points. The Kaplan-Meier data show the two year probability of C-N-S relapse rises from roughly two to three percent in the low risk group, to around four to five percent in intermediate risk, up to approximately twelve percent in the high risk group. Critically, once C-N-S relapse occurs, overall survival is dismal, dropping sharply within the first several months, which is why identifying high risk patients matters, since it guides decisions about C-N-S directed prophylaxis such as intrathecal or high dose methotrexate.

keypoints: CNS-IPI = 5 classic IPI factors plus kidney or adrenal involvement (1 point each)
Risk groups: low 0-1, intermediate 2-3, high 4-6
CNS relapse probability rises from ~2-3% (low) to ~12% (high risk)
OS after CNS relapse occurs is very poor, dropping sharply within months
High CNS-IPI score guides decisions on CNS-directed prophylaxis
segments.voiceover: The C-N-S I-P-I is simply the five I-P-I factors plus kidney or adrenal involvement, giving three risk groups, low, intermediate, and high. High risk patients have roughly a twelve percent chance of C-N-S relapse, versus only two to three percent in low risk, and this score is what guides the decision to add C-N-S prophylaxis, since survival after a C-N-S relapse is extremely poor.

The Hans algorithm is the immunohistochemistry surrogate used to classify diffuse large B cell lymphoma into germinal center B cell, or G-C-B, versus non-germinal center subtypes, approximating the more expensive gene expression profiling. It is a sequential three stain algorithm: first stain for C-D-ten; if positive, the tumor is classified G-C-B. If C-D-ten is negative, stain for B-C-L-six; if B-C-L-six is also negative, the tumor is non-G-C. If B-C-L-six is positive, stain for M-U-M-one; M-U-M-one positive calls it non-G-C, while M-U-M-one negative calls it G-C-B. In the original validation cohort, non-G-C-B patients had significantly worse overall survival than G-C-B patients, with a highly significant p value. On the molecular side, gene expression profiling separates D-L-B-C-L not otherwise specified into G-C-B, activated B cell or A-B-C, an unclassified group, and primary mediastinal B cell lymphoma, and more recent genomic classification schemes further subdivide these into subtypes like E-Z-B, B-N-two, M-C-D, and N-one, each with characteristic mutations, for example M-Y-D-eighty-eight L-two-six-five-P and C-D-seventy-nine A or B alterations in M-C-D, that point toward rational targeted therapies such as B-C-R pathway or B-C-L-two inhibitors.

keypoints: Hans algorithm: CD10 positive = GCB; CD10 negative + BCL6 negative = non-GCB
CD10 negative + BCL6 positive: MUM1 positive = non-GCB, MUM1 negative = GCB
Non-GCB has significantly worse overall survival than GCB (P<.001)
Gene expression profiling splits DLBCL into GCB, ABC, unclassified, and PMBL
Genetic subtypes (EZB, BN2, MCD, N1) carry distinct mutations and suggest targeted agents
segments.voiceover: For boards, memorize the Hans algorithm sequence: C-D-ten first, then B-C-L-six, then M-U-M-one if needed, sorting tumors into G-C-B or non-G-C-B. Non-G-C-B carries a worse prognosis. Beyond immunohistochemistry, know that gene expression profiling defines G-C-B, A-B-C, and primary mediastinal subtypes, and that newer genomic classifiers like E-Z-B and M-C-D refine this further and can point toward specific targeted agents.

This slide distinguishes double hit from double expresser lymphoma, a common point of confusion on boards. Double hit lymphoma is a genetic diagnosis, defined by concurrent rearrangement of M-Y-C together with B-C-L-two, or less commonly B-C-L-six, detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization, F-I-S-H. These rearrangements cluster mostly within the germinal center B cell subtype. Double expresser lymphoma, by contrast, is a protein level, immunohistochemistry based diagnosis, defined simply by high expression of both M-Y-C and B-C-L-two proteins, regardless of whether the underlying gene rearrangements are present, and it can occur in either germinal center or activated B cell subtypes. Prognostically these are distinct: in the referenced cohort, classical diffuse large B cell lymphoma without either feature had the best overall survival, roughly sixty percent at long term follow up; double expresser lymphoma had intermediate outcomes; and double hit lymphoma had the worst outcomes, with survival curves separating early and significantly, p less than zero point zero zero one for double hit versus classical, and p equals zero point zero one four for double expresser versus classical. Reflecting this biology, the WHO twenty twenty two classification renamed double hit as diffuse large B cell lymphoma or high grade B cell lymphoma with M-Y-C and B-C-L-two rearrangements, while the I-C-C twenty twenty two classification calls it high grade B cell lymphoma with M-Y-C and B-C-L-two rearrangements.

keypoints: Double hit lymphoma: concurrent MYC plus BCL2 (or BCL6) rearrangement, confirmed by FISH
Double expresser lymphoma: high MYC and BCL2 protein by IHC, without requiring gene rearrangement
Outcome ranking: classical DLBCL best, double expresser intermediate, double hit worst (P<.001, P=.014)
WHO 2022 and ICC 2022 both reclassify double hit as high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements
segments.voiceover: Do not confuse these two entities. Double hit is a genetic, F-I-S-H based diagnosis, M-Y-C plus B-C-L-two rearrangement, and carries the worst prognosis. Double expresser is a protein, immunohistochemistry based diagnosis, high M-Y-C and B-C-L-two expression without necessarily having the rearrangement, and it carries an intermediate prognosis, worse than classical D-L-B-C-L but better than double hit. Both the WHO and I-C-C twenty twenty two classifications now formally recognize double hit as its own high grade B cell lymphoma category.

This is the first-line therapy algorithm for stage one and two DLBCL, excluding stage two with extensive mesenteric disease. The first branch point is bulk, nonbulky meaning less than seven point five centimeters versus bulky at seven point five centimeters or greater. The second branch point is the stage-modified International Prognostic Index, the smIPI, which is built from age over sixty, elevated LDH, poor performance status, and stage two or IIE disease, with zero to one point called low risk and two to four called high risk. For nonbulky, low-risk smIPI disease, the pathway is short, R-CHOP for three cycles, then interim restaging with PET-CT. If that PET is negative, you either give one more cycle of R-CHOP for a total of four, or you consolidate with involved-site radiotherapy and then observe. Nonbulky high-risk smIPI disease gets rerouted to follow the same pathway as stage two with extensive mesenteric disease or stage three-four. Bulky, low-risk disease gets a slightly longer course, R-CHOP for three to four cycles, then interim PET-CT restaging. And stage two with extensive mesenteric disease, or stage three-four disease, goes straight to the suggested regimens table for first-line therapy, followed by interim restaging with PET-CT or CT after two to four cycles.

keypoints: Two branch points: bulk (<7.5cm vs ≥7.5cm) and stage-modified IPI (0-1 low vs 2-4 high)
smIPI factors: age >60, LDH elevated, poor performance status, stage II/IIE
Nonbulky, smIPI 0-1: R-CHOP x3 → interim PET/CT → PET negative gets R-CHOP x1 more or ISRT then observe
Bulky, smIPI 0-1: R-CHOP x3-4 → interim PET/CT restaging
smIPI >1, extensive mesenteric disease, or stage III-IV all follow the same higher-risk pathway
segments.voiceover: Remember the two branch points, bulk versus nonbulky at the seven point five centimeter cutoff, and the stage-modified IPI, which is age over sixty, elevated LDH, poor performance status, and stage two or IIE disease. Low risk is zero to one factor, high risk is two to four. Nonbulky, low-risk patients get the shortest course, R-CHOP times three, then interim PET-CT, and if negative, just one more cycle or radiotherapy and observation. Bulky, low-risk patients get three to four cycles before restaging. Anyone with high-risk smIPI, extensive mesenteric disease, or stage three-four disease funnels into the higher-risk pathway with the suggested regimens table.

This is the suggested treatment regimens table for first-line DLBCL therapy, and it's organized by clinical scenario rather than by stage alone. For stage one to two, excluding extensive mesenteric disease, the options are CHOP plus rituximab, or Pola-R-CHP, that's polatuzumab vedotin added to CHP plus rituximab, reserved for smIPI greater than one, both category one. For stage two with extensive mesenteric disease or stage three to four, CHOP plus rituximab and Pola-R-CHP for IPI two or higher remain preferred and category one, with dose-adjusted EPOCH plus rituximab as another recommended option. Two special populations get their own columns. Patients with poor left ventricular function need anthracycline-sparing or anthracycline-modified regimens, DA-EPOCH-R, CDOP which substitutes liposomal doxorubicin, CEOP which drops the anthracycline entirely, or GCVP with gemcitabine. Very frail patients and those over eighty with comorbidities get attenuated regimens, CDOP, mini-CHOP, or GCVP, all with rituximab. At the bottom, there's a dedicated box for concurrent CNS disease. Parenchymal CNS involvement is treated with systemic high-dose methotrexate at three grams per meter squared or higher, integrated into an anthracycline cycle, with the panel preferring day fifteen of a twenty-one day cycle. Leptomeningeal disease is treated with intrathecal cytarabine, methotrexate, and hydrocortisone, often through an Ommaya reservoir, plus systemic high-dose methotrexate, and consolidation with high-dose therapy and autologous stem cell rescue can be considered.

keypoints: Stage I-II: CHOP+R or Pola-R-CHP (smIPI >1), category 1
Stage II extensive mesenteric or III-IV: CHOP+R or Pola-R-CHP (IPI ≥2) preferred, category 1; DA-EPOCH+R also recommended
Poor LV function: anthracycline-sparing options, DA-EPOCH-R, CDOP, CEOP, GCVP + rituximab
Frail or age >80 with comorbidities: attenuated regimens, CDOP, mini-CHOP, GCVP + rituximab
CNS disease: high-dose methotrexate for parenchymal, IT triple therapy plus systemic methotrexate for leptomeningeal, consider HDT/ASCR consolidation
segments.voiceover: Match the regimen to the clinical scenario. Standard-risk stage one to two gets CHOP plus rituximab, or Pola-R-CHP if smIPI is greater than one. Higher-stage or bulky mesenteric disease gets the same backbone or dose-adjusted EPOCH. Poor cardiac function pushes you toward anthracycline-sparing regimens like CDOP or CEOP, while frailty or advanced age pushes you toward attenuated dosing like mini-CHOP. And for concurrent CNS disease, remember the two-tier approach, high-dose methotrexate integrated into chemotherapy for parenchymal disease, and intrathecal triple therapy plus systemic methotrexate for leptomeningeal disease.

This is the five-year update of the POLARIX trial, comparing Pola-R-CHP against standard R-CHOP in the global intention-to-treat population, four hundred forty patients versus four hundred thirty-nine. Look at how the two progression-free survival curves separate early and then stay apart. At the primary analysis, two years, event-free rate was seventy-six point seven percent with Pola-R-CHP versus seventy point two percent with R-CHOP, a hazard ratio of zero point seven three. At the three-year update, seventy-one point eight versus sixty-four point one percent, hazard ratio zero point seven six. And now at the five-year update, sixty-four point nine percent versus fifty-nine point one percent, hazard ratio zero point seven seven. Notice the hazard ratio barely moves across three separate readouts, which tells you this isn't an early effect that washes out, it's a durable, sustained separation. This is the trial that justified moving polatuzumab vedotin into the first-line, category one option for higher-risk DLBCL, specifically smIPI greater than one or IPI two or higher, as you saw on the previous regimens slide.

keypoints: POLARIX: Pola-R-CHP (n=440) vs R-CHOP (n=439) in the global ITT population
PFS benefit favors Pola-R-CHP at 2, 3, and 5 years — HR stays stable, 0.73 to 0.77
5-year PFS: 64.9% (Pola-R-CHP) vs 59.1% (R-CHOP)
Durable separation of curves supports category 1 status for Pola-R-CHP in higher-risk first-line DLBCL
segments.voiceover: The key number to remember is the hazard ratio, roughly zero point seven three to zero point seven seven, and it stays essentially flat from the two-year primary analysis all the way to the five-year update. That durability is what earned Pola-R-CHP its category one first-line status for smIPI greater than one or IPI two or higher DLBCL. Five-year PFS lands at about sixty-five percent with Pola-R-CHP versus fifty-nine percent with R-CHOP.

This is second-line therapy for relapsed disease within twelve months, or primary refractory disease, and the whole table is split by one question, is the patient a CAR T-cell candidate? On the candidate side, CAR T-cell therapy itself, either axicabtagene ciloleucel or lisocabtagene maraleucel, both CD19-directed and both category one, is the therapy. Around that core, there's holding therapy to bridge patients before pheresis, and bridging therapy to bridge them after pheresis while waiting for the CAR T product to be manufactured, options like DHAP, GDP, GEMOX, ICE, polatuzumab vedotin plus rituximab, or involved-site radiotherapy. On the non-candidate side, you're choosing among newer targeted combinations and older platinum-based salvage regimens. Preferred options include GEMOX combined with the bispecific antibodies epcoritamab or glofitamab, GEMOX plus polatuzumab and rituximab, lenalidomide plus tafasitamab excluding primary refractory disease, polatuzumab with or without bendamustine and rituximab, and mosunetuzumab or glofitamab paired with polatuzumab. Other recommended options are the classic salvage regimens, CEOP, DHAP, ESHAP, GDP, GEMOX, and ICE. And there's a useful-in-certain-circumstances category for brentuximab vedotin, ibrutinib in non-germinal center DLBCL, and lenalidomide with or without rituximab, also non-GCB.

keypoints: Split by CAR T-cell candidacy: this defines the entire second-line pathway for early relapse or primary refractory disease
Candidates: axi-cel or liso-cel (CD19-directed, category 1), with holding and bridging chemo around pheresis
Non-candidates preferred: GEMOX + epcoritamab or glofitamab, GEMOX + Pola + R, lenalidomide + tafasitamab, Pola ± bendamustine + R
Classic salvage regimens (CEOP, DHAP, ESHAP, GDP, ICE) are now second-tier, not first choice
Non-GCB DLBCL: consider ibrutinib or lenalidomide as niche options
segments.voiceover: The whole table hinges on one question, CAR T candidate or not. If yes, axi-cel or liso-cel is the answer, bridged with platinum-based chemo like DHAP or GDP, or with polatuzumab and rituximab. If not a candidate, the preferred options have shifted toward bispecific antibodies paired with GEMOX, or polatuzumab-based combinations, pushing older regimens like ICE and ESHAP down to secondary status. Keep ibrutinib and lenalidomide in your back pocket specifically for non-germinal center DLBCL.

Now compare this to relapse after twelve months, which is a fundamentally different clinical situation because late relapses behave more like a second chance at cure with conventional salvage and transplant. This table splits by intention to proceed to transplant rather than by CAR T eligibility. If transplant is intended, the preferred regimens are the familiar platinum-based salvage backbones, DHAP, GDP, or ICE, each with or without rituximab, with ESHAP and GEMOX as other recommended options, all aiming to get the patient into a good enough response to proceed to autologous transplant. If there's no intention to proceed to transplant, the preferred list looks much more like the primary refractory pathway you just saw, CAR T-cell therapy with lisocabtagene maraleucel if eligible, GEMOX plus epcoritamab or glofitamab, GEMOX plus polatuzumab and rituximab, lenalidomide plus tafasitamab, polatuzumab-based combinations, and the bispecific plus polatuzumab pairings. Other recommended options are CEOP, GDP, GEMOX, or rituximab alone, and the same useful-in-certain-circumstances list applies, brentuximab vedotin, ibrutinib, and lenalidomide for non-GCB disease.

keypoints: Late relapse, over twelve months, is split by transplant intention, not CAR T eligibility
Transplant intended: classic platinum-based salvage, DHAP, GDP, or ICE ± rituximab, to bridge to autologous transplant
No transplant intended: CAR T-cell therapy (liso-cel) or novel antibody combinations become preferred, similar to the primary refractory pathway
The clinical logic: late relapse still favors chemo-sensitive salvage and transplant as first choice when feasible
segments.voiceover: The key distinction from the last slide is timing. Relapse after twelve months is treated as potentially curable with conventional salvage chemo followed by autologous transplant, so DHAP, GDP, or ICE are preferred when transplant is intended. Only when transplant isn't intended do you pivot to the same CAR T and bispecific antibody options used for early relapse or primary refractory disease.

This is third-line and subsequent therapy, and the note at the top is important, any second-line regimen the patient hasn't already received can still be reused here. The preferred column is built around T-cell mediated therapy. CAR T-cell therapy is preferred, and this slide has been annotated to show a real guideline update, lisocabtagene maraleucel is struck through and tisagenlecleucel has been added in its place alongside axicabtagene ciloleucel, both CD19-directed. That's a detail worth knowing for boards, which specific CAR T products are approved shifts as trials mature and labels change, so don't over-anchor on any single product list. Alongside CAR T, bispecific antibody therapy, epcoritamab or glofitamab, is preferred, and importantly these are usable even in patients who progressed after transplant or after CAR T-cell therapy, which matters because that's a group with very few options otherwise. The other recommended column has three distinct mechanisms, lenalidomide plus brentuximab vedotin plus rituximab, loncastuximab tesirine, an antibody-drug conjugate, and selinexor, a nuclear export inhibitor, which is also explicitly usable after transplant or CAR T failure.

keypoints: Unused second-line regimens remain valid options at third-line
Preferred: CAR T-cell therapy (axi-cel, tisagenlecleucel) and bispecific antibodies (epcoritamab, glofitamab)
Slide shows an annotated guideline update, liso-cel struck out, tisagenlecleucel added — CAR T product lists change over time
Bispecifics and selinexor remain usable even after CAR T or transplant failure
Other recommended: lenalidomide + brentuximab vedotin + rituximab, loncastuximab tesirine, selinexor
segments.voiceover: Third-line therapy centers on T-cell engaging approaches, CAR T-cell therapy and bispecific antibodies like epcoritamab and glofitamab, both of which remain options even after a patient has already failed transplant or CAR T. Notice the annotated edit on this slide, liso-cel crossed out and tisagenlecleucel added, a reminder that specific product recommendations evolve. For patients who've exhausted T-cell approaches, loncastuximab tesirine and selinexor are the fallback mechanisms to know.

Let's switch gears to primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma, PMBCL, a distinct entity that boards love to test because it breaks the usual DLBCL pattern in almost every way. The typical patient is young, around thirty-five, with a strong female predominance, which is unusual for lymphoma in general. It presents as a bulky anterior mediastinal mass that locally invades the lung, pleura, and pericardium, and can encase or compress the superior vena cava, so think of a young woman presenting with SVC syndrome or a large mediastinal mass on chest imaging. Genetically, PMBCL has its own distinct expression profile, but here's the twist, it actually shares more in common with classic Hodgkin lymphoma than with typical DLBCL, both arise from thymic B cells and share pathways like PD-L1 and PD-L2 amplification at 9p24. For treatment, response to intensive chemotherapy is good, R-CHOP or a stronger regimen like dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab. The relapsed and refractory setting is genuinely controversial, if the post-treatment PET scan is negative, observation alone is a reasonable strategy rather than reflexive consolidation. PET is essential after treatment to guide that decision, and overall, PMBCL carries a more favorable prognosis than typical DLBCL. The inset box on the right shows the commonly used first-line options, dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab for six cycles, R-CHOP-14 for four to six cycles, or R-CHOP-21 for six cycles, all followed by PET-CT restaging.

keypoints: PMBCL: young patients (~35), female predominance, bulky anterior mediastinal mass with SVC encasement
Distinct gene expression profile from DLBCL but shares biology with classical Hodgkin lymphoma
Treatment: intensive chemo (R-CHOP or DA-EPOCH-R) gives good response; relapsed/refractory management is controversial
Post-treatment PET is essential; if PET-negative, observation alone is reasonable
Overall prognosis is more favorable than typical DLBCL
segments.voiceover: PMBCL is the classic board vignette, a young woman with a bulky anterior mediastinal mass and possible SVC syndrome. Remember it's biologically closer to classical Hodgkin lymphoma than to typical DLBCL, despite being treated as a B-cell lymphoma. First-line options are R-CHOP or dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab, and the critical decision point after treatment is the PET scan, a negative PET supports observation without radiation. Overall, prognosis is better than standard DLBCL.

This slide shows the pivotal New England Journal of Medicine paper behind dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab in PMBCL, the Dunleavy study that established this regimen as a chemotherapy-alone option, without consolidative mediastinal radiation. The four panels show event-free and overall survival separately for the NCI cohort and the Stanford validation cohort. Look at how flat and high these curves stay out to ten-plus years, there's an early drop in the first year or so in the NCI cohort, reflecting the handful of early treatment failures, but after that the curve barely moves, and the Stanford cohort curves are essentially flat from the start. The headline numbers on the right say it clearly, five-year progression-free survival of ninety-three percent and five-year overall survival of ninety-seven percent, achieved with chemotherapy alone. This is the evidence base for the practice you just learned, treat with dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab, restage with PET, and if the scan is clean, you can often avoid radiation entirely, sparing young patients, who are disproportionately young women, from the long-term cardiac and breast cancer risks of mediastinal radiotherapy.

keypoints: Landmark NEJM study establishing dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab for PMBCL without radiation
5-year PFS 93%, 5-year OS 97%, chemotherapy alone
Curves stay flat after an early first-year drop, validated across NCI and Stanford cohorts
Rationale: avoiding radiation spares young, predominantly female patients from long-term cardiac and breast cancer risk
segments.voiceover: This is the trial to cite when you're asked why PMBCL can be treated without radiation. Dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab alone achieved five-year progression-free survival of ninety-three percent and overall survival of ninety-seven percent, validated in both the NCI and Stanford cohorts. That outcome is why a PET-negative scan after chemo supports skipping radiotherapy, which matters most because these patients are young and disproportionately female, exactly the population most vulnerable to radiation's late cardiac and breast cancer risks.

Primary CNS lymphoma is a distinct entity worth knowing cold for boards. Ninety-five percent are diffuse large B cell lymphoma, and specifically the activated B cell, or ABC, subtype, which tends to behave more aggressively than germinal center type. Median age at diagnosis is sixty. Here's a testable epidemiologic shift: incidence has actually declined in HIV positive patients thanks to antiretroviral therapy, but it's been rising in immunocompetent patients, so don't assume this is only an immunosuppression-related disease anymore. Ocular involvement matters too, intraocular lymphoma accounts for ten to twenty percent of cases, and you should always get a slit lamp exam. Sixteen percent have concurrent leptomeningeal involvement, so CSF cytology and flow cytometry are part of the workup. Extraneural, meaning systemic, disease is uncommon, only four to twelve percent, and B symptoms like fever, night sweats, and weight loss are extremely uncommon, unlike systemic DLBCL. On immunohistochemistry, BCL6 is positive in sixty to eighty percent, while CD10 positivity is much lower, only ten to twenty percent, reflecting a mostly non-germinal-center immunophenotype.

keypoints: PCNSL: 95% DLBCL, ABC subtype, median age 60
Incidence rising in immunocompetent, declining in HIV-positive patients
Intraocular involvement 10-20%, leptomeningeal 16%, extraneural rare (4-12%)
B symptoms extremely uncommon (unlike systemic DLBCL)
BCL6+ in 60-80%, CD10+ in only 10-20%
segments.voiceover: Remember PCNSL as ninety-five percent DLBCL, ABC subtype, median age sixty. Incidence is falling in HIV positive patients but rising in the immunocompetent. Watch for intraocular involvement in ten to twenty percent, leptomeningeal spread in sixteen percent, and rare extraneural disease. B symptoms are unusual here. Immunophenotype is BCL6 positive sixty to eighty percent, CD10 positive only ten to twenty percent.

This is the International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group prognostic system, the go-to risk score for primary CNS lymphoma, and it's a favorite exam topic. Five adverse factors are counted: age over sixty, ECOG performance status greater than two, elevated LDH, high CSF protein, and tumor location in the deep brain structures like the periventricular region, basal ganglia, brainstem, or cerebellum. Patients are stratified by how many of these five factors they have. With zero risk factors, two year overall survival is excellent, around eighty percent. With one to four factors, it drops substantially to forty-eight percent. And with all five factors present, survival craters to just fifteen percent. The Kaplan-Meier curves from the original Ferreri study, published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology in 2003, show a highly significant separation between these three risk groups, with a p value of 0.00001. This score helps guide prognosis discussions and clinical trial stratification in PCNSL.

keypoints: IELSG score: age >60, PS >2, high LDH, high CSF protein, deep brain lesion
0 risk factors: 2yr OS ~80%
1-4 risk factors: 2yr OS ~48%
5 risk factors: 2yr OS only 15%
Ferreri et al, JCO 2003; highly significant risk stratification (p=0.00001)
segments.voiceover: Know the five IELSG factors: age over sixty, poor performance status, elevated LDH, high CSF protein, and deep brain location. Zero factors gives roughly eighty percent two year survival, one to four factors gives forty-eight percent, and all five factors gives just fifteen percent. This is a classic board question about PCNSL prognosis.

This NCCN table maps out systemic therapy for primary CNS lymphoma across three phases. For induction, the preferred backbone is high dose methotrexate at eight grams per meter squared combined with rituximab, often paired with leucovorin and temozolomide, or in the MPV regimen with procarbazine and vincristine. A lower dose methotrexate option exists too, usually paired with consideration of whole brain radiotherapy. MATRIX, which adds cytarabine and thiotepa to methotrexate and rituximab, is another recommended option. For consolidation, the preferred approach is high dose therapy with autologous stem cell rescue, using conditioning regimens like cytarabine and thiotepa followed by carmustine and thiotepa, or the TBC regimen. Alternatives include etoposide with high dose cytarabine, or monthly maintenance methotrexate-based therapy, or temozolomide alone. For relapsed or refractory disease, options are broad: retreatment with methotrexate-based regimens, ibrutinib combinations, temozolomide, rituximab, pemetrexed, lenalidomide, pomalidomide, and even CAR T-cell therapy with tisagenlecleucel as a category 2B option. Notably, a phase one-two study of the BTK inhibitor tirabrutinib in relapsed refractory PCNSL showed an overall response rate of sixty-three point six percent, with a duration of response of nine point two months and progression free survival of two point nine months.

keypoints: Induction: HD-methotrexate 8g/m2 + rituximab, ± temozolomide or MPV/MT combinations
Consolidation: high dose therapy with autologous stem cell rescue preferred
Alternative consolidation: EA, high dose cytarabine, or maintenance methotrexate/rituximab
Relapsed/refractory: ibrutinib combos, temozolomide, lenalidomide, tisagenlecleucel (CAR-T)
Tirabrutinib trial: ORR 63.6%, DOR 9.2 months, PFS 2.9 months
segments.voiceover: For PCNSL, induction centers on high dose methotrexate plus rituximab. Consolidation preferentially uses autologous stem cell transplant, with chemo-only or maintenance as alternatives. For relapse, think BTK inhibitors like ibrutinib, temozolomide, lenalidomide, and CAR T-cell therapy. And remember the tirabrutinib data, response rate about sixty-four percent, but short duration of response.

Burkitt lymphoma is the single most aggressive B cell lymphoma, but also one of the most curable when treated correctly. Nearly one hundred percent of cells are Ki-67 positive, reflecting an extremely high proliferation rate. The defining molecular lesion is c-MYC overexpression, most commonly from the t 8;14 translocation involving the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, seen in about eighty percent of cases, with the remainder driven by light chain partners, t 2;8 with kappa or t 8;22 with lambda. The typical immunophenotype is surface immunoglobulin positive, CD10 positive, CD20 positive, TdT negative, Ki-67 positive at ninety-five percent or higher, BCL2 negative, and BCL6 positive. Cytogenetically it's usually a simple karyotype with the MYC rearrangement as the sole abnormality, which helps distinguish it from double-hit lymphomas. There are three clinical subtypes: endemic, sporadic, and HIV-related. Clinically, expect a bulky abdominal mass, B symptoms, and bone marrow involvement in about seventy percent of cases. The endemic African form classically presents with a jaw or facial mass in children.

keypoints: Most aggressive B-cell lymphoma; Ki-67 near 100%
MYC-driven: t(8;14) IGH in 80%; light chain variants t(2;8), t(8;22)
Immunophenotype: CD10+, CD20+, BCL2-, BCL6+, TdT-; simple karyotype
Endemic (jaw mass), sporadic, and HIV-related subtypes
Bulky abdominal mass; marrow involvement ~70%
segments.voiceover: Burkitt lymphoma is the most aggressive B cell lymphoma, driven by MYC rearrangement, usually t 8;14 with the immunoglobulin heavy chain in eighty percent. Immunophenotype is CD10 positive, BCL2 negative, BCL6 positive, with a simple karyotype. Know the three subtypes, endemic with jaw masses, sporadic, and HIV-related, and remember the classic bulky abdominal presentation with high marrow involvement.

Treatment of Burkitt lymphoma is risk-adapted, and the single most important point for boards is this: CHOP is not adequate therapy, it under-treats this highly proliferative disease. Risk stratification starts with low risk, defined as normal LDH plus stage one disease with a single extra-abdominal mass under ten centimeters, or a completely resected abdominal lesion. High risk includes stage one with an abdominal mass, an extra-abdominal mass over ten centimeters, or stage two through four disease. For patients under sixty who are low risk, options include CODOX-M with intrathecal chemotherapy, dose-adjusted EPOCH plus rituximab guided by interim PET response, or HyperCVAD alternating with cytarabine and high dose methotrexate plus rituximab. High risk patients, especially those with symptomatic CNS disease, need regimens with strong CNS penetration, such as CODOX-M alternating with IVAC, or HyperCVAD, both with intrathecal therapy, or dose-adjusted EPOCH-R for those who can't tolerate more aggressive approaches. For patients sixty and older, low risk patients get DA-EPOCH plus rituximab guided by PET, while high risk older patients get dose-adjusted EPOCH-R with intensive intrathecal methotrexate for CNS disease.

keypoints: CHOP is NOT adequate therapy for Burkitt lymphoma
Low risk: normal LDH, stage I, small or completely resected mass
High risk: abdominal mass, mass >10cm, or stage II-IV disease
Younger patients: CODOX-M, DA-EPOCH-RR, or HyperCVAD + rituximab
CNS disease requires CNS-penetrating regimens plus intrathecal chemo
segments.voiceover: The key testable point is that CHOP is inadequate for Burkitt lymphoma. Risk stratification depends on LDH, stage, and mass size and location. Younger low risk patients get CODOX-M, dose-adjusted EPOCH-RR, or HyperCVAD. High risk or CNS-involved patients need CNS-penetrating regimens with intrathecal chemotherapy built in.

This slide shows the landmark long-term outcomes for dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab in Burkitt lymphoma from Dunleavy and colleagues, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2013. In HIV-negative patients treated with DA-EPOCH-R, at a median follow-up of eighty-six months, freedom from progression was ninety-five percent and overall survival was essentially one hundred percent. That's a remarkable result for such an aggressive lymphoma using a relatively lower-intensity, outpatient-friendly regimen compared to HyperCVAD-type approaches. Even more striking, in HIV-positive patients treated with the short-course variant, SC-EPOCH-RR, at a median follow-up of seventy-three months, freedom from progression was one hundred percent and overall survival was ninety-five percent. The Kaplan-Meier curves confirm durable, essentially flat survival plateaus in both cohorts. This data helped establish dose-adjusted EPOCH-R as a highly effective, less toxic alternative to intensive regimens like HyperCVAD or CODOX-M slash IVAC for Burkitt lymphoma, in both HIV-negative and HIV-positive populations.

keypoints: DA-EPOCH-R (HIV-negative): 86-month follow-up, FFP 95%, OS 100%
SC-EPOCH-RR (HIV-positive): 73-month follow-up, FFP 100%, OS 95%
Dose-adjusted EPOCH-R gives durable cures with less toxicity than HyperCVAD-type regimens
Dunleavy et al, NEJM 2013
segments.voiceover: Dose-adjusted EPOCH-rituximab produces excellent outcomes in Burkitt lymphoma, roughly ninety-five to one hundred percent freedom from progression and overall survival in both HIV-negative and HIV-positive patients, per Dunleavy's NEJM 2013 paper. This is a lower-intensity alternative to HyperCVAD that still cures nearly everyone.
Now let's shift gears to follicular lymphoma, the second most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma and the prototype of indolent B cell lymphomas.

Follicular lymphoma has a median age of about sixty and, interestingly, is less common in Asian and African American populations compared to Caucasians, a demographic point that occasionally shows up on exams. Biologically it's extremely sensitive to both radiation and chemotherapy, which is why localized disease can sometimes be cured with radiation alone. There's a notable association with hepatitis C infection, and in those patients, treating the underlying hepatitis C with interferon and ribavirin can actually induce lymphoma regression. Clinically, patients present with lymphadenopathy, but B symptoms like fever, night sweats, and weight loss are uncommon, seen in only about ten percent. Splenomegaly is present in roughly half of patients. The molecular hallmark is the t 14;18 translocation involving BCL2, found in about eighty-five percent of cases, leading to BCL2 overexpression and resistance to apoptosis. Despite this, only fifteen to thirty percent of patients present with early stage, localized disease, most present with advanced stage at diagnosis. The immunophenotype is CD10 positive, BCL2 positive, BCL6 positive, CD20 positive, with CD23 variable, and importantly CD43 negative and CD5 negative, which helps distinguish it from mantle cell and CLL slash SLL.

keypoints: Median age ~60; less common in Asian and African American patients
Highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive; hepatitis C linked, responds to IFN/ribavirin
t(14;18) BCL2 translocation in ~85% of cases
Only 15-30% present at early stage; splenomegaly in ~50%
Immunophenotype: CD10+, BCL2+, BCL6+, CD20+, CD5-, CD43-
segments.voiceover: Follicular lymphoma presents around age sixty, is highly sensitive to radiation and chemo, and has a hepatitis C association that can respond to antiviral therapy. The molecular hallmark is t 14;18 with BCL2 in about eighty-five percent of cases. Most patients present with advanced, not early, stage disease. And remember the immunophenotype, CD10 positive, BCL2 positive, BCL6 positive, but CD5 and CD43 negative, distinguishing it from mantle cell lymphoma.

This slide covers prognostic scoring systems for follicular lymphoma. The FLIPI, or Follicular Lymphoma International Prognostic Index, comes in two versions. FLIPI-1 uses five adverse factors, easily remembered by the mnemonic No LASH, meaning number of nodal sites greater than four, elevated LDH, age over sixty, advanced stage III or IV, and hemoglobin under twelve. Patients with zero to one factor are low risk, two factors intermediate risk, and three to five factors high risk. FLIPI-2 modifies this slightly, replacing nodal site number with maximal lymph node diameter over six centimeters, replacing LDH with beta-2 microglobulin, and replacing Ann Arbor stage with bone marrow involvement. On the right, the PRIMA-PI score is a simpler two-step tool using beta-2 microglobulin and bone marrow involvement. If beta-2 microglobulin is above three milligrams per liter, the patient is high risk. If it's three or below, bone marrow involvement determines whether the patient is intermediate or low risk. For boards, remember No LASH for FLIPI-1 and know that PRIMA-PI is a streamlined alternative built around beta-2 microglobulin and marrow status.

keypoints: FLIPI-1 mnemonic: No LASH, nodal sites, LDH, age, stage, hemoglobin
FLIPI-2 swaps in lymph node size, beta-2 microglobulin, marrow involvement
Risk groups: zero to one low, two intermediate, three to five high
PRIMA-PI uses beta-2 microglobulin plus marrow involvement
segments.voiceover: Remember FLIPI-1 with the mnemonic No LASH, number of nodal sites, LDH, age, stage, and hemoglobin. FLIPI-2 replaces some of those with lymph node size, beta-2 microglobulin, and bone marrow involvement. Risk stratifies into low, intermediate, and high groups. And PRIMA-PI offers a quicker two-variable approach using beta-2 microglobulin and marrow involvement.

This algorithm outlines management of grade one to two follicular lymphoma based on stage and tumor burden. For limited stage disease, options include involved-site radiotherapy, anti-CD20 therapy with or without radiation, or immunochemotherapy with or without radiation. For advanced stage, stage two bulky, or B-symptomatic disease, the next branch point is tumor burden. Asymptomatic patients with low tumor burden can be managed with watchful waiting or immediate rituximab, since studies show no survival difference between the two approaches, though watch and wait avoids unnecessary treatment toxicity. Symptomatic patients with high tumor burden require active treatment. Tumor burden itself is defined by the GELF criteria, which the table lists, any nodal or extranodal mass greater than seven centimeters, three or more nodal sites larger than three centimeters, elevated LDH, hemoglobin under ten, absolute neutrophil count under one point five, platelets under one hundred, splenomegaly greater than sixteen centimeters by CT, risk of organ compression, or significant serous effusions. Knowing these criteria helps decide who needs treatment versus who can be safely observed.

keypoints: Limited stage: involved-site RT, anti-CD20, or immunochemotherapy
Advanced stage guided by symptoms and tumor burden
Low burden, asymptomatic: watch and wait or immediate rituximab
High burden or symptomatic disease requires active treatment
GELF criteria define high tumor burden
segments.voiceover: For limited stage follicular lymphoma, treat with radiotherapy or anti-CD20-based therapy. For advanced disease, asymptomatic low tumor burden patients can be watched or given rituximab alone, while symptomatic high tumor burden patients need active treatment. High tumor burden is defined by the GELF criteria, covering large masses, multiple nodal sites, elevated LDH, cytopenias, splenomegaly, organ compression, or effusions.

This slide compares two important first-line trials in indolent lymphoma. On the left, the German StiL NHL 1-2003 trial randomized five hundred forty-nine patients with follicular, Waldenstrom's, marginal zone, mantle cell, or small lymphocytic lymphoma to bendamustine plus rituximab versus R-CHOP. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival, and bendamustine-rituximab showed a strikingly longer median PFS of about sixty-nine and a half months compared to just over thirty-one months with R-CHOP, a hazard ratio of zero point five eight. This established B-R as a preferred first-line regimen with a more favorable toxicity profile. On the right, the GALLIUM trial tested obinutuzumab-based chemoimmunotherapy against rituximab-based chemoimmunotherapy, both followed by maintenance, in over twelve hundred treatment-naive patients with indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma including follicular lymphoma. Investigator-assessed three-year progression-free survival favored the obinutuzumab arm, eighty percent versus seventy-three percent, with a hazard ratio of zero point six six. Together these trials support both bendamustine-rituximab as a backbone regimen and obinutuzumab as a potentially superior anti-CD20 partner for chemoimmunotherapy.

keypoints: StiL trial: bendamustine-rituximab beat R-CHOP in PFS
B-R median PFS about seventy months versus thirty-one months for R-CHOP
GALLIUM: obinutuzumab plus chemo versus rituximab plus chemo
Obinutuzumab arm had better three-year PFS, eighty versus seventy-three percent
segments.voiceover: The StiL trial showed bendamustine-rituximab significantly outperforms R-CHOP in progression-free survival for indolent lymphomas, making B-R a preferred first-line backbone. The GALLIUM trial showed obinutuzumab-based chemoimmunotherapy edges out rituximab-based therapy, with three-year PFS of eighty percent versus seventy-three percent.

This slide addresses maintenance therapy for symptomatic, high tumor burden follicular lymphoma. Maintenance rituximab is individualized, and there's a lack of data beyond two years of use. The pivotal PRIMA trial randomized patients responding to rituximab plus chemotherapy to receive rituximab maintenance every two months for two years versus observation. The event-free survival curves on the left, panel C, show a clear benefit for maintenance, with a hazard ratio of zero point six two and a p-value of zero point zero zero zero four. However, panel D, which represents a different outcome measure, shows nearly overlapping curves with a hazard ratio close to one, zero point eight seven, and a non-significant p-value of zero point six zero. So the key takeaway for boards is that PRIMA showed rituximab maintenance improves progression-free or event-free survival but does not translate into an overall survival benefit, which is why maintenance decisions should be individualized based on patient factors and shared decision-making.

keypoints: PRIMA trial: rituximab maintenance every two months for two years
Maintenance improved event-free survival, hazard ratio zero point six two
No overall survival benefit was seen
Maintenance decisions should be individualized
segments.voiceover: The PRIMA trial established that two years of rituximab maintenance after response to R-chemo improves progression-free survival, but it does not improve overall survival. Because of this, and limited data beyond two years, maintenance therapy should be individualized for each patient.

This slide highlights two recent phase three trials, both published in the Lancet in January 2026, evaluating novel agents added to lenalidomide and rituximab for relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma. On the left, the EPCORE FL-1 trial compared epcoritamab, a CD20 by CD3 bispecific antibody, plus lenalidomide and rituximab, against lenalidomide and rituximab alone. Progression-free survival was dramatically improved in the epcoritamab arm, with the median not yet reached compared to eleven point seven months in the control arm, a hazard ratio of zero point two one. On the right, the inMIND trial tested tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 monoclonal antibody, added to lenalidomide and rituximab, against placebo plus lenalidomide and rituximab. Median progression-free survival was twenty-two point four months with tafasitamab versus thirteen point nine months with placebo, a hazard ratio of zero point four three. Both trials demonstrate that adding a novel targeted agent, whether a bispecific antibody or an anti-CD19 antibody, to lenalidomide-rituximab substantially improves outcomes in relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma, reflecting the rapidly evolving treatment landscape fellows should be aware of for boards.

keypoints: EPCORE FL-1: epcoritamab plus len-R versus len-R alone
Epcoritamab arm PFS not reached versus eleven point seven months
inMIND: tafasitamab plus len-R versus placebo plus len-R
Tafasitamab arm median PFS twenty-two point four versus thirteen point nine months
segments.voiceover: Two new phase three trials show major PFS benefit when adding novel agents to lenalidomide-rituximab in relapsed refractory follicular lymphoma. Epcoritamab, a bispecific antibody, in EPCORE FL-1 gave a hazard ratio of zero point two one. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, in inMIND gave a hazard ratio of zero point four three. Both represent important additions to the relapsed refractory treatment armamentarium.

This is the NCCN suggested treatment regimen table for follicular lymphoma, organized by line of therapy. First-line therapy for high tumor burden includes bendamustine, CHOP, or CVP combined with obinutuzumab or rituximab, plus lenalidomide-rituximab as an alternative. For low tumor burden, single-agent rituximab is preferred. Optional first-line extended therapy, meaning maintenance, includes rituximab every eight to twelve weeks for two years after chemoimmunotherapy, or obinutuzumab maintenance. For older or infirm patients unable to tolerate combination therapy, single-agent rituximab is preferred. Second-line therapy largely mirrors first-line chemoimmunotherapy options, but now also includes the novel combinations we just discussed, lenalidomide-rituximab plus epcoritamab, or lenalidomide-rituximab plus tafasitamab, both category one recommendations. Other second-line options include single-agent lenalidomide, obinutuzumab, or rituximab. Second-line extended therapy again offers rituximab or obinutuzumab maintenance. Third-line and subsequent therapy opens up to T-cell mediated approaches, including bispecific antibodies like epcoritamab or mosunetuzumab, and CAR T-cell therapies such as axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, or tisagenlecleucel.
