Very good partial response is a ninety percent or greater M protein drop, partial response is fifty percent or greater, and minimal response is twenty five to forty nine percent. Stringent complete response adds a normal free light chain ratio on top of complete response.

This continues the response criteria, now covering disease progression and relapse. Stable disease is not used as a formal response category, since time to progression better captures it. Progressive disease requires a twenty five percent increase from the lowest confirmed value, with an absolute serum M protein rise of at least zero point five grams per deciliter, or an absolute urine M protein rise of at least two hundred milligrams per day, along with alternatives for free light chains, bone marrow plasma cell percentage, new lesions, or a fifty percent increase in circulating plasma cells. Clinical relapse is a distinct, practical category requiring new CRAB features or organ dysfunction, new plasmacytomas or bone lesions, a definite fifty percent increase in existing lesion size, hypercalcemia over eleven, a hemoglobin drop of two grams per deciliter or more, a creatinine rise of two milligrams per deciliter or more, or hyperviscosity. Relapse from complete response or from MRD negative status requires reappearance of the M protein, five percent or more bone marrow plasma cells, or any new sign of progression such as a new plasmacytoma.

keypoints: Stable disease is not used as a formal response category; time-to-progression is preferred instead
Progressive disease: 25% relative increase from nadir with defined absolute thresholds in M protein, FLC, or marrow plasma cells
Progressive disease also includes new lesions or a 50% or more increase in circulating plasma cells
Clinical relapse: new CRAB features, new plasmacytomas, hypercalcemia, anemia, renal decline, or hyperviscosity
Relapse from CR or MRD-negative status: reappearing M protein, 5% or more marrow plasma cells, or a new progression sign
segments.voiceover: For exam purposes, remember progressive disease is a twenty five percent relative increase with a defined absolute threshold, half a gram per deciliter for serum M protein or two hundred milligrams a day for urine. Clinical relapse is the practical bedside category, driven by new CRAB features, new lesions, or hyperviscosity. And relapse from complete response or MRD negativity is confirmed by a reappearing M protein or five percent or more marrow plasma cells.

This flowchart, from the Taiwan Society of Hematology multiple myeloma guideline, outlines the initial treatment pathway for newly diagnosed disease. After diagnosis, every patient is assessed for disease burden, performance status, organ function, comorbidities, cytogenetics by FISH, and staging, and clinical trial enrollment should always be considered if available. The central decision point is transplant eligibility. Transplant eligible patients receive a triplet or quadruplet combining a proteasome inhibitor and an immunomodulatory drug for three to six induction cycles, followed by high dose melphalan conditioning and autologous stem cell transplant, then optional consolidation and maintenance therapy. In select cases, if a patient is concerned about high dose chemotherapy toxicity and induction has already achieved a deep response, transplant can be deferred. Transplant ineligible patients instead receive a doublet, triplet, or quadruplet PI and or IMiD based regimen continued as ongoing therapy. Both pathways converge at relapse, which triggers subsequent line therapy.

keypoints: Transplant eligibility is the key branch point after initial disease assessment
Transplant-eligible: PI/IMiD triplet or quadruplet induction for 3-6 cycles, then autologous stem cell transplant
Post-transplant: optional consolidation followed by maintenance therapy
Transplant-ineligible: continuous PI and/or IMiD-based doublet, triplet, or quadruplet therapy
Transplant can be deferred if induction achieves a deep response and the patient wants to avoid high-dose chemo toxicity
segments.voiceover: The core decision for newly diagnosed myeloma is transplant eligibility. Eligible patients get induction with a PI plus IMiD, high dose melphalan, autologous transplant, then maintenance, with consolidation as an option in between. Ineligible patients get continuous combination therapy without transplant. Both pathways eventually meet at relapse, prompting subsequent line therapy, and transplant can occasionally be deferred if induction already achieves a deep response.

This slide details primary induction regimens for transplant eligible newly diagnosed myeloma, combining NCCN preferred regimens with a Taiwanese reimbursement algorithm. The NCCN preferred triplet regimens are daratumumab, lenalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone, or isatuximab, bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone, both category one. Other recommended options include bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone, carfilzomib based triplets, and daratumumab or isatuximab added to carfilzomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone. The Taiwan flowchart shows treatment choice depends on insurance coverage, patient preference, comorbidities, renal function, neuropathy, hematopoietic reserve, tumor aggressiveness, and extramedullary disease. For triplets, proteasome inhibitor plus IMiD combinations like VTD or RVD are the current first line mainstay, while PI alone with VCD, or IMiD alone with CTD, are used in select circumstances. For quadruplet therapy, daratumumab VTd or daratumumab VRd are now reimbursed by Taiwan's national health insurance as of September twenty twenty five, with VTDC or PACE based regimens reserved for aggressive or refractory presentations.

keypoints: NCCN preferred triplets: daratumumab or isatuximab plus bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone, both category 1
PI plus IMiD triplets like VTD and RVD are the current first-line mainstay
PI-only (VCD) or IMiD-only (CTD) triplets are reserved for select circumstances
Quadruplet Dara-VTd or Dara-VRd gained Taiwan NHI reimbursement in September 2025
PACE-based regimens (VTD-PACE, VRD-PACE) are reserved for aggressive or high-risk disease
segments.voiceover: For boards, the preferred induction for transplant eligible patients is a daratumumab or isatuximab based triplet with a proteasome inhibitor, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone. PI plus IMiD combinations like VTD and RVD remain the first line mainstay. Quadruplet daratumumab regimens are increasingly standard and now reimbursed in Taiwan as of late twenty twenty five, while PACE based regimens are reserved for aggressive disease.

This slide covers autologous stem cell transplant and the consolidation that can follow it. For the conditioning regimen going into autologous transplant, high dose melphalan remains the standard, typically dosed at one forty to two hundred milligrams per square meter of body surface area. Tandem autologous transplant, meaning a planned second transplant within six months of the first, isn't for everyone. Current evidence suggests it benefits two groups in particular, patients who fail to reach at least a very good partial response, or VGPR, within three months of their first transplant, and patients who present with high risk cytogenetics at diagnosis. In both groups, tandem transplant appears to improve both response depth and overall survival, though case selection really matters here. Moving to consolidation after autologous transplant, the general approach is to give two to four additional cycles using a regimen similar to what the patient received during induction. This is recommended specifically for patients who still haven't achieved a VGPR after transplant. Timing matters too, consolidation should ideally start within one to two months after transplant, and should not be delayed beyond three months.

keypoints: Standard conditioning is high dose melphalan at 140 to 200 mg per m squared
Tandem autologous transplant benefits patients without VGPR by 3 months post-transplant
High-risk cytogenetics at diagnosis also favors tandem transplant
Consolidation gives 2 to 4 cycles similar to induction if VGPR not reached
Start consolidation within 1 to 2 months, no later than 3 months post-transplant
segments.voiceover: To recap, high dose melphalan is the conditioning backbone for autologous transplant, and tandem transplant is reserved for patients without VGPR at three months or those with high risk cytogenetics. Consolidation, when used, mirrors the induction regimen for two to four cycles and should start within one to two months, no later than three months after transplant.

This slide details post transplant maintenance therapy. Recommended options include thalidomide at fifty to one hundred milligrams daily, lenalidomide at ten to twenty five milligrams daily, though this isn't yet first line reimbursed, or the maximum dose an individual patient can tolerate. Proteasome inhibitors can also serve as maintenance, bortezomib for example can be given every two weeks at one point three milligrams per square meter. Based on clinical trial data, patients who received daratumumab as part of first line therapy may also continue it as maintenance, dosed roughly every one to two months, though this again lacks health insurance reimbursement currently. Maintenance is generally continued until disease progression or unacceptable drug related toxicity. It's worth noting the literature suggests long term lenalidomide maintenance may increase the risk of second primary malignancies, but international consensus still holds that the benefits outweigh the risks, so physicians should discuss this tradeoff with patients. For proteasome inhibitor based maintenance, two years of treatment can be considered. Timing wise, maintenance should begin within one to two months after autologous transplant or consolidation, ideally no later than three months. The NCCN table below reinforces lenalidomide as the preferred category one maintenance option, with carfilzomib plus lenalidomide or daratumumab plus lenalidomide as other recommended choices, and bortezomib, daratumumab alone, or ixazomib reserved for certain circumstances.

keypoints: Lenalidomide is preferred maintenance, thalidomide and bortezomib are alternatives
Daratumumab maintenance is an option after frontline use, not yet reimbursed
Continue maintenance until progression or intolerable toxicity
Long-term lenalidomide raises secondary malignancy risk but benefit outweighs risk
Start maintenance within 1 to 2 months post-transplant, no later than 3 months
segments.voiceover: Remember lenalidomide is the preferred maintenance agent per NCCN, with bortezomib, daratumumab, and ixazomib as alternatives in select patients. Watch for the secondary malignancy risk with long term lenalidomide, and start maintenance promptly, within one to two months of finishing transplant or consolidation.

This flowchart addresses first line therapy for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma patients who are not transplant candidates. Treatment choice depends on insurance coverage rules, patient preference, comorbidities, renal function, neurologic status, hematopoietic reserve, tumor aggressiveness, presence of extramedullary disease, and physician preference. Options are organized by number of drug classes combined, quadruplet, triplet, or doublet regimens. Among quadruplets, daratumumab VMP and VMPT exist, though VMPT isn't considered mainstream. For triplets, the combination of a proteasome inhibitor plus an immunomodulatory drug, currently the mainstream first line approach, includes VRd, RVD-lite for frailer patients, and VTD. Proteasome inhibitor only triplets include VCD and VMP. Immunomodulatory drug based triplets include daratumumab-Rd as an option, while CTd, CRd, MPT, and MPR are non-mainstream alternatives used in select situations. Doublets split into proteasome inhibitor based, such as VD, or immunomodulatory drug based, such as Rd or TD. The NCCN table on this slide echoes this hierarchy, with the preferred category one regimens being daratumumab-lenalidomide-dexamethasone, daratumumab-bortezomib-lenalidomide-dexamethasone for non-frail patients under eighty, and isatuximab-bortezomib-lenalidomide-dexamethasone under similar criteria.

keypoints: Non-transplant first line therapy is chosen based on comorbidities and frailty
PI plus IMiD triplets like VRd are the current first line mainstream
Quadruplets like daratumumab VMP exist but VMPT is not mainstream
NCCN preferred regimens are Dara-Rd, Dara-VRd, and Isa-VRd, category 1
Doublets such as VD or Rd are reserved for frailer or less aggressive disease
segments.voiceover: Key takeaway here, PI plus IMiD triplets such as VRd represent the current mainstream first line approach for transplant ineligible patients, and NCCN ranks daratumumab or isatuximab based quadruplets as preferred category one options for appropriately selected patients, while doublets are reserved for frail patients.

This diagram outlines management of first relapse or disease progression, essentially second line therapy. If a clinical trial is available, that should be considered first. From there, treatment branches along three main axes. The first asks whether the patient has not yet received an anti-CD38 antibody, or has not become refractory to one. If naive or still sensitive, treatment proceeds with an anti-CD38 antibody based regimen, daratumumab options include DRd, DVd, or DKd, while isatuximab options include isatuximab-Kd or isatuximab-Pd. If the patient has already become refractory to anti-CD38 therapy, selection then depends on prior exposure to bortezomib and lenalidomide, if neither has failed, VRd can be used, if bortezomib has failed, options include elotuzumab-Rd, elotuzumab-Pd, PCd, Pd, or Kd, and if lenalidomide has failed, options include pomalidomide-Vd, elotuzumab-Pd, PCd, Pd, or Kd. The second axis is high risk cytogenetics, defined as deletion 17p, t four fourteen, t fourteen sixteen, or 1q21 amplification, for which IRd is recommended. The third axis covers extramedullary relapse or plasma cell leukemia, managed with aggressive chemotherapy regimens like DCEP or DT-PACE and VTD-PACE, or allogeneic transplant if the patient's condition allows and no better alternative exists.

keypoints: Consider a clinical trial first at relapse if available
Anti-CD38 naive or sensitive patients get daratumumab or isatuximab based regimens
Anti-CD38 refractory patients are chosen based on prior bortezomib and lenalidomide exposure
High-risk cytogenetics including del 17p and t four fourteen favor IRd
Extramedullary relapse or plasma cell leukemia needs aggressive chemo or allo transplant
segments.voiceover: For first relapse, remember the decision tree branches on anti-CD38 antibody exposure status, high risk cytogenetics pointing toward IRd, and extramedullary or plasma cell leukemia relapse requiring aggressive PACE-based chemotherapy or consideration of allogeneic transplant.

This algorithm addresses management of multiply relapsed myeloma, organizing options by drug class backbone rather than by prior exposure alone, since by this point patients have typically cycled through several drug classes already. Choices should still weigh insurance coverage, patient preference, comorbidities, renal function, neurologic status, hematopoietic reserve, tumor aggressiveness, and extramedullary disease. The anti-CD38 antibody based branch splits into daratumumab, giving DRd, daratumumab-pomalidomide-dexamethasone, DVd, or DKd, and isatuximab, giving isatuximab-Kd or isatuximab-pomalidomide-dexamethasone. The pomalidomide based branch includes Pd, PCd, pomalidomide-Vd, or elotuzumab-Pd. The carfilzomib based branch includes Kd or KCd. The lenalidomide based branch includes IRd or elotuzumab-Rd. And the other category captures clinical trials, compassionate use programs, DCEP, bendamustine, cyclophosphamide, or melphalan combinations, selinexor, allogeneic transplant if appropriate, bispecific antibodies, and CAR T cell therapy. A note on this slide flags that as of 2026, several of these agents, particularly the bispecifics and CAR T products, now have partial reimbursement or expanded insurance coverage that wasn't previously available.

keypoints: Multiple relapse regimens are chosen by drug class backbone, not just prior lines
Anti-CD38 branch splits into daratumumab and isatuximab combinations
Other options include selinexor, allo transplant, bispecifics, and CAR T
By 2026 several novel agents have gained partial reimbursement
segments.voiceover: For multiply relapsed disease, organize your thinking around drug class backbones, anti-CD38, pomalidomide, carfilzomib, or lenalidomide based combinations, and know that bispecific antibodies and CAR T cell therapy now sit in the toolbox with expanding reimbursement as of 2026.

This table summarizes the first choice bispecific antibody regimens for multiply relapsed or refractory myeloma. Teclistamab, studied in the MajesTEC-1 trial, uses step up dosing, point zero six milligrams per kilogram on day one, point three milligrams per kilogram on day four, spaced two to seven days apart, followed by the standard weekly dose of one point five milligrams per kilogram starting two to seven days after the final step up dose. It's FDA approved for fifth line or later therapy and gained Taiwan FDA approval, and as of May first, twenty twenty five, it's now covered by national health insurance. Elranatamab, from the MagnetisMM-3 trial, is given subcutaneously with step up dosing of twelve milligrams per kilogram on day one and thirty two milligrams per kilogram on day four, at least two days apart, then a standard dose of seventy six milligrams weekly starting day eight for twenty four weeks, after which responders can switch to dosing every two weeks. It also became health insurance covered as of May first, twenty twenty five. Talquetamab, from the MonumenTAL-1 trial, offers weekly or every two week subcutaneous dosing, point four milligrams per kilogram weekly or point eight milligrams per kilogram every two weeks, each with its own step up schedule. It's FDA approved for fifth line therapy and has Taiwan FDA approval, though it isn't yet covered by national health insurance.

keypoints: Teclistamab, elranatamab, and talquetamab use step-up dosing to reduce cytokine release syndrome
All three are FDA approved for fifth line or later relapsed refractory myeloma
Teclistamab and elranatamab gained Taiwan health insurance coverage May 2025
Talquetamab has Taiwan FDA approval but is not yet reimbursed
segments.voiceover: Key point here, all three T cell redirecting bispecifics, teclistamab, elranatamab, and talquetamab, use step up dosing to mitigate cytokine release syndrome, and while all are FDA approved for late line disease, only teclistamab and elranatamab currently have Taiwan health insurance coverage.

This slide reviews two pivotal trials for belantamab mafodotin, an antibody drug conjugate targeting BCMA. DREAMM-7 compared belantamab mafodotin plus bortezomib and dexamethasone, or BVd, against daratumumab plus bortezomib and dexamethasone, or DVd. The results were striking, median progression free survival was thirty six point six months with BVd versus thirteen point four months with DVd, a hazard ratio of zero point four one, highly statistically significant. DREAMM-8 compared belantamab mafodotin plus pomalidomide and dexamethasone against pomalidomide plus bortezomib and dexamethasone, again showing a clear benefit with a hazard ratio of zero point five two. Both trials, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in June twenty twenty four, support belantamab mafodotin combinations as effective options in relapsed disease. On the safety side, all grade adverse events with these combinations included thrombocytopenia in eighty seven percent, ocular adverse events in seventy nine percent, upper respiratory infection in twenty percent, anemia in nineteen percent, and pneumonia in eighteen percent. The ocular toxicity is a hallmark and defining side effect of belantamab mafodotin, presenting as keratopathy, or changes to the corneal epithelium, blurred vision, and dry eye. In these trials these events were managed with dose delays and reductions, and despite how common they were, permanent treatment discontinuation due solely to ocular toxicity was relatively uncommon.

keypoints: DREAMM-7 showed BVd had median PFS of 36.6 months versus 13.4 months for DVd
DREAMM-8 showed belantamab-pomalidomide-dexamethasone outperformed PVd, HR 0.52
Ocular toxicity, especially keratopathy, is the hallmark side effect of belantamab mafodotin
Ocular events are managed with dose delays and reductions rather than discontinuation
segments.voiceover: Remember belantamab mafodotin combinations dramatically improved progression free survival in both DREAMM-7 and DREAMM-8, but the tradeoff is a very high rate of ocular toxicity, especially keratopathy, which is managed with dose modification rather than stopping the drug outright in most patients.

This slide features the MajesTEC-3 trial, published in December twenty twenty five, which compared teclistamab plus daratumumab against standard daratumumab-pomalidomide-dexamethasone or daratumumab-bortezomib-dexamethasone in relapsed refractory myeloma. The overall survival benefit was substantial, thirty six month overall survival was eighty three point three percent with teclistamab-daratumumab compared to sixty five percent with the standard regimens, a highly significant difference. Alongside this trial data, the slide shows the NCCN recommendations for therapy after three or more prior lines of treatment. CAR T cell therapy, either ciltacabtagene autoleucel or idecabtagene vicleucel, is preferred. After at least four prior therapies including an anti-CD38 antibody, a proteasome inhibitor, and an immunomodulatory drug, bispecific antibodies become preferred options, elranatamab, linvoseltamab, talquetamab, and teclistamab. Other recommended options include high dose or fractionated cyclophosphamide, and after four or more prior therapies with refractoriness to at least two proteasome inhibitors, two immunomodulatory agents, and an anti-CD38 antibody, selinexor plus dexamethasone is an option. Finally, useful in certain circumstances includes belantamab mafodotin, bendamustine based combinations, and combining talquetamab with teclistamab.

keypoints: MajesTEC-3 showed teclistamab-daratumumab improved 36-month OS to 83.3% vs 65%
CAR T-cell therapy is preferred after 3 or more prior lines of therapy
Bispecific antibodies are preferred after 4+ lines including anti-CD38, PI, and IMiD exposure
Selinexor-dexamethasone is an option for penta-refractory disease
segments.voiceover: Take away that MajesTEC-3 demonstrated a clear overall survival advantage for teclistamab plus daratumumab, and that NCCN now positions CAR T cell therapy as preferred after three or more prior lines, with bispecific antibodies preferred once patients are refractory to an anti-CD38 antibody, a PI, and an IMiD.

This slide covers two board-relevant myeloma supportive care topics: bone disease management and infection prophylaxis. For skeletal-related events, NCCN guidelines say every myeloma patient getting active treatment should receive a bone-targeted agent, either a bisphosphonate or denosumab, though local reimbursement may restrict coverage to those with proven lytic disease. Before starting, get a dental exam and clear any needed dental work first, because these drugs carry a jaw osteonecrosis risk; avoid procedures like extractions or implants for ninety days around dosing. Zoledronic acid is four milligrams IV over at least fifteen minutes, dose-adjusted for renal function and held if creatinine clearance is under thirty; denosumab is one hundred twenty milligrams subcutaneous every four weeks and is the preferred option in renal impairment since it isn't renally cleared. Bisphosphonate therapy is typically capped around two years, though continuation is a shared decision; denosumab is generally continued longer, sometimes spaced to every six months, and stopping it requires a bisphosphonate dose afterward to prevent rebound osteoporosis. Meanwhile, all patients should be screened for hepatitis B and C before first-line therapy. Anyone on a proteasome inhibitor, an anti-CD38 or anti-SLAMF7 antibody, a bispecific, CAR-T, or a recent autologous transplant needs herpes zoster and HSV prophylaxis with valacyclovir, acyclovir, or famcyclovir, especially if seropositive. Antifungal prophylaxis with fluconazole or an echinocandin is considered for severe mucositis or neutropenia under five hundred for more than a week post-transplant.

keypoints: Bone-targeted therapy: bisphosphonate or denosumab for all active-treatment myeloma patients
Dental exam before starting; avoid dental procedures 90 days around dosing (osteonecrosis risk)
Denosumab preferred if CrCl under 30; stopping it needs a bisphosphonate dose to prevent rebound osteoporosis
Screen hepatitis B and C before first-line therapy
Antiviral prophylaxis with PI, CD38/SLAMF7 antibody, CAR-T, or after autologous transplant
segments.voiceover: Remember three exam pearls. First, all myeloma patients on active treatment get a bone-targeted agent, dental clearance first, and a ninety-day dental procedure blackout around dosing. Second, denosumab is preferred when renal function is poor, and stopping it needs a bisphosphonate dose to prevent rebound osteoporosis. Third, screen hepatitis B and C up front, and give herpes prophylaxis with proteasome inhibitors, CD38 antibodies, bispecifics, CAR-T, or after autologous transplant.

This slide bundles the myeloma vaccination schedule with anemia and cytopenia management. On vaccines, influenza is annual for everyone and publicly funded. Pneumococcal vaccination uses the sequential strategy: PCV13 first, one dose, then PPV23 at least one year later, though high-risk patients can shorten that gap to eight weeks; PPV23 itself can be repeated after five years, but public funding is generally limited to age sixty-five and up. Zoster vaccination is recommended for everyone, but only the non-live recombinant subunit vaccine, since these patients are immunocompromised, and it's self-pay. COVID-19 follows the rolling national guidance. For anemia, if a myeloma patient has symptomatic anemia with hemoglobin persistently under ten and no other identifiable cause, consider an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, erythropoietin alfa forty thousand units weekly or erythropoietin beta thirty thousand units weekly, especially with concurrent renal impairment or low endogenous erythropoietin. Target hemoglobin should stay under twelve, and if there's no response after six to eight weeks, stop the ESA rather than escalating. Because anti-CD38 antibodies like daratumumab and isatuximab interfere with the indirect antiglobulin test and confound blood typing, get a type and screen before starting these drugs. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor is used for neutropenia per standard practice, but thrombopoietin receptor agonists for myeloma-related thrombocytopenia aren't recommended yet given limited clinical data.

keypoints: Pneumococcal: PCV13 first, then PPV23 at least 1 year later (8 weeks if high-risk); repeat PPV23 at 5 years
Zoster vaccine must be non-live recombinant (immunocompromised patients); self-pay
ESA for symptomatic anemia with Hb under 10 and no other cause; target Hb under 12, stop if no response by 6-8 weeks
Type and antibody screen BEFORE anti-CD38 therapy, since daratumumab/isatuximab interfere with crossmatch
G-CSF standard for neutropenia; TPO receptor agonists not recommended for myeloma thrombocytopenia
segments.voiceover: Three testable points. Pneumococcal vaccination is sequential, PCV13 then PPV23 at least a year later, and zoster vaccine must be the non-live recombinant form because these patients are immunocompromised. For anemia, ESAs target hemoglobin under twelve and get stopped if there's no response by six to eight weeks. And always pull a type and antibody screen before starting anti-CD38 therapy, since daratumumab and isatuximab interfere with the indirect Coombs test.

This next section is a grab-bag labeled simply Others, covering miscellaneous high-yield topics outside the main lymphoma and myeloma algorithms, think Castleman disease and CAR-T toxicity management, both of which show up regularly on boards.

This diagnostic algorithm is the board-favorite approach to Castleman disease. It starts with Castleman-like lymph node histology on biopsy, which by itself isn't diagnostic, you must first exclude other disease-associated causes, and the slide groups these into three buckets worth memorizing: infectious causes like EBV, mycobacteria, toxoplasmosis, and CMV; autoimmune and inflammatory causes like IgG4-related disease, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and adult-onset Still's disease; and neoplastic mimics like Kaposi sarcoma, mantle or marginal zone lymphoma, and germinotropic lymphoproliferative disorder. Once those are excluded, CT with or without PET defines the distribution and guides further biopsy, splitting patients into unicentric Castleman disease, a single nodal region, versus multicentric Castleman disease, multiple regions. Multicentric disease then branches three ways based on etiology: HHV-8-associated MCD, typically in HIV-positive or immunocompromised patients; POEMS-associated MCD, tied to the polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M protein, skin changes syndrome; and idiopathic MCD, or iMCD, when HHV-8 and POEMS are both ruled out. iMCD then splits further into iMCD-NOS and iMCD-TAFRO, the latter being the aggressive variant with thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, and organomegaly, a distinction that matters a lot for prognosis and urgency of treatment.

keypoints: Castleman-like histology is nonspecific; must exclude infectious, autoimmune/inflammatory, and neoplastic mimics first
CT plus or minus PET defines distribution, splitting unicentric (UCD) from multicentric (MCD)
MCD subtypes: HHV8-MCD, POEMS-MCD, and idiopathic MCD (iMCD)
iMCD splits into iMCD-NOS and iMCD-TAFRO (thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, organomegaly)
TAFRO is the aggressive, high-mortality iMCD variant
segments.voiceover: The algorithm in three steps. First, Castleman-like histology needs exclusion of infectious, autoimmune, and neoplastic mimics before you call it Castleman disease. Second, imaging distribution splits unicentric from multicentric disease. Third, multicentric disease branches into HHV-8-associated, POEMS-associated, or idiopathic, and idiopathic MCD further splits into NOS and the aggressive TAFRO variant, which stands for thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, and organomegaly.

This is the treatment algorithm for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease, and it's risk-stratified by five severity criteria: ECOG performance status two or worse, renal failure with GFR under thirty, anemia with hemoglobin under eight, widespread serous effusions, and pulmonary involvement. Zero out of five criteria means asymptomatic disease, and the answer is simply observation, no treatment, just regular monitoring for progression. One out of five criteria is non-severe disease, and first-line therapy is siltuximab, an anti-IL-6 monoclonal antibody, with or without oral steroids, or alternatively thalidomide plus rituximab with or without steroids. If that gives an adequate response, you move to maintenance siltuximab or thalidomide; if inadequate, escalate to combination chemotherapy. Two or more out of five criteria defines severe disease, including TAFRO syndrome, and that demands anti-IL-6 therapy plus high-dose parenteral steroids, or combination chemotherapy like R-CHOP or R-CVP. A good response there gets maintenance siltuximab, while an inadequate response should prompt referral to clinical trials, since options run out fast at that severity tier. The key teaching point is that siltuximab, targeting IL-6, is the backbone first-line agent across the non-severe and severe pathways, reflecting IL-6's central role in iMCD pathophysiology.

keypoints: 5 severity criteria: ECOG 2 or worse, renal failure (GFR under 30), anemia (Hb under 8), serous effusions, pulmonary involvement
0/5 criteria = asymptomatic, observation only
1/5 criteria = non-severe, siltuximab with or without steroids, or thalidomide plus rituximab with or without steroids
2 or more/5 criteria = severe (including TAFRO), anti-IL-6 plus high-dose steroids or combination chemo (R-CHOP/R-CVP)
Siltuximab (anti-IL-6) is the backbone agent, reflecting IL-6-driven pathophysiology
segments.voiceover: Stratify by five criteria: ECOG, renal failure, anemia, effusions, and pulmonary involvement. Zero criteria means observe only. One criterion is non-severe, treated with siltuximab or thalidomide-rituximab. Two or more, including TAFRO, is severe and needs anti-IL-6 therapy with high-dose steroids or combination chemotherapy. Across the board, siltuximab targeting IL-6 is the first-line backbone because IL-6 drives iMCD pathophysiology.

This table is the ASTCT consensus grading for cytokine release syndrome, a must-know for CAR-T boards. Fever, defined as temperature at least thirty-eight degrees Celsius, is required for every grade, that's the entry criterion. Grade one is fever alone, no hypotension, no hypoxia. Grade two adds hypotension not requiring vasopressors, and or hypoxia requiring low-flow oxygen at six liters per minute or less, or blow-by oxygen. Grade three steps up to hypotension requiring a single vasopressor, with or without vasopressin, and or hypoxia requiring high-flow oxygen above six liters per minute, face mask, non-rebreather mask, or Venturi mask. Grade four is the most severe: hypotension requiring multiple vasopressors, excluding vasopressin, and or hypoxia requiring positive pressure ventilation such as CPAP, BiPAP, intubation, or mechanical ventilation. The pattern to memorize is that hypotension severity tracks vasopressor need, none, one, multiple, while hypoxia severity tracks oxygen delivery method, low-flow, high-flow, positive pressure, and grade is driven by the worse of the two parameters, not an average.

keypoints: Fever at least 38C required at every grade (entry criterion)
Grade 1: fever only; Grade 2: hypotension without pressors and/or hypoxia needing 6L/min or less low-flow O2
Grade 3: hypotension needing 1 vasopressor and/or hypoxia needing more than 6L/min high-flow O2 or mask
Grade 4: hypotension needing multiple vasopressors (excluding vasopressin) and/or hypoxia needing positive pressure ventilation
Overall grade is driven by the worse of the hypotension or hypoxia parameter
segments.voiceover: Fever is required at every grade. Then hypotension severity tracks vasopressor need, none for grade one, one agent for grade three, multiple for grade four, while hypoxia severity tracks oxygen delivery, from low-flow to high-flow to positive pressure ventilation. The overall grade is set by whichever parameter, hypotension or hypoxia, is worse.

This flowchart operationalizes CRS management by grade. Grades two through four all trigger an ICU notification, and every grade gets blood cultures, an infectious workup, prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics, and supportive symptom management like antipyretics and fluid resuscitation. Starting at grade two, and continuing through grades three and four, you initiate specific CRS-directed therapy, which for higher grades means completing IV tocilizumab at eight milligrams per kilogram, capped at eight hundred milligrams, before transferring the patient to the ICU. If grade two worsens, add dexamethasone ten milligrams every six hours for one to three days; if it progresses further, escalate to dexamethasone twenty milligrams every six hours for three days with a taper over three to seven days. If there's no improvement twelve hours after the first tocilizumab dose, repeat tocilizumab at the same weight-based dose. For grade one with no improvement after three days and no alternative diagnosis, consider tocilizumab as well, though it's a lower urgency pathway. If symptoms persist despite dexamethasone and repeat tocilizumab, the algorithm escalates to high-dose methylprednisolone: one thousand milligrams daily for three days, then tapering through two hundred fifty milligrams twice daily, one twenty-five twice daily, and sixty twice daily, each step for two days. And critically, repeat tocilizumab dosing should only be considered if the patient has not developed ICANS, since IL-6 blockade can theoretically worsen neurotoxicity.

keypoints: Grade 2-4 CRS triggers ICU notification; all grades get cultures, prophylactic antibiotics, supportive care
Tocilizumab 8mg/kg (max 800mg) IV completed before ICU transfer for higher grades
Escalating dexamethasone: 10mg every 6h, then 20mg every 6h with taper if worsening
No improvement 12h after tocilizumab, repeat the tocilizumab dose
Refractory disease escalates to high-dose methylprednisolone taper; repeat tocilizumab only if no ICANS present
segments.voiceover: ICU notification kicks in at grade two and up, alongside cultures and prophylactic antibiotics for every grade. Tocilizumab at eight milligrams per kilogram is the first specific therapy, escalating dexamethasone if it worsens, and repeating tocilizumab if there's no improvement at twelve hours. Refractory cases move to high-dose methylprednisolone with a taper. Remember, repeat tocilizumab is only appropriate if the patient hasn't developed ICANS.

This slide covers the ICE score, the Immune Effector Cell-associated Encephalopathy assessment tool used to grade CAR-T neurotoxicity, or ICANS. It's a ten-point scale built from five domains. Orientation is worth four points: can the patient state the year, month, city, and hospital. Naming is worth three points: can they name three objects, like a clock, a pen, and a button. Following commands is worth one point, such as holding up two fingers or closing the eyes and sticking out the tongue. Writing a standard sentence is worth one point. And attention, counting backward from one hundred by tens, is worth one point. Four plus three plus one plus one plus one gets you to ten total. The grading cutoffs matter for boards: a score of seven to nine is grade one, three to six is grade two, zero to two is grade three, and if the patient can't be aroused enough to complete the ICE assessment at all, that's automatically grade four, regardless of score. Combine this with seizure activity, elevated intracranial pressure, and motor findings from the full ASTCT ICANS grading system, but the ICE score itself is the piece most likely to be tested directly.

keypoints: ICE score is a 10-point tool: orientation (4), naming (3), commands (1), writing (1), attention (1)
Score 7-9 = grade 1; 3-6 = grade 2; 0-2 = grade 3
Cannot be aroused to perform the ICE assessment = automatic grade 4
ICE score is the core component of ASTCT ICANS grading for CAR-T neurotoxicity
segments.voiceover: The ICE score totals ten points across orientation, naming, commands, writing, and attention. Seven to nine is grade one, three to six is grade two, zero to two is grade three, and an unarousable patient who can't even attempt the test is automatic grade four. This is the core tool for grading CAR-T associated neurotoxicity, ICANS.

This table lays out the ASTCT consensus grading for ICANS, the immune effector cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome that fellows will see after CAR T cell therapy or bispecific antibody treatment for lymphoma. Grading runs across five domains. First, the ICE score, that's the immune effector cell encephalopathy score, used for patients twelve and older, where a score of seven to nine is grade one, three to six is grade two, zero to two is grade three, and a score of zero with the patient unarousable and unable to be tested is grade four. Second, level of consciousness, ranging from spontaneous awakening in grade one, down to arousal only with vigorous or repetitive tactile stimuli, or stupor and coma, in grade four. Third, seizures, which only enter the picture at grade three, with any seizure that resolves quickly, and grade four, with life threatening prolonged seizures lasting more than five minutes or repetitive seizures without return to baseline. Fourth, motor findings, which only appear at grade four, as deep focal motor weakness such as hemiparesis or paraparesis. And fifth, signs of raised intracranial pressure or cerebral edema, appearing at grade three as focal edema on imaging, and at grade four as decerebrate or decorticate posturing, sixth nerve palsy, papilledema, Cushing's triad, or diffuse cerebral edema. The overall ICANS grade is set by the most severe domain present.

keypoints: ASTCT ICANS grading uses five domains
ICE score defines grades one through four in adults
Seizures and motor weakness only appear at grade three and four
Overall grade equals the worst affected domain
segments.voiceover: Remember, ICANS grading follows five domains: ICE score, consciousness, seizures, motor findings, and intracranial pressure signs. The ICE score anchors grading in patients twelve and older, from seven to nine at grade one down to zero at grade four. Seizures and focal motor weakness only enter at grade three and four. And critically, the overall grade is always set by whichever domain is most severe.

This flowchart shows how to manage ICANS once you've assigned a grade. For grade one, close monitoring is sufficient, along with workup such as EEG, MRI, and lumbar puncture to rule out other causes. From grade two onward, you notify the ICU and involve neurology, consider holding oral intake and switching medications to intravenous formulations, and for grade three and four you should strongly consider ICU transfer. Across grades two through four, in the absence of contraindications, pursue EEG, MRI, and lumbar puncture for differential diagnosis. Outside of clinical trials, ICANS specific therapies remain limited. One key pearl here, when grade one CRS occurs together with grade two or higher ICANS, steroids rather than tocilizumab are the appropriate treatment, though that approach is not suitable for more severe CRS. If seizures occur, clinically or on EEG, give levetiracetam and benzodiazepines, and if seizures persist or recur, repeat benzodiazepines, otherwise treat as status epilepticus. Standard therapy is intravenous dexamethasone ten milligrams every six hours for one to three days. If there is cerebral edema, consider hyperosmolar therapy. If the patient worsens, escalate to intravenous methylprednisolone, one thousand milligrams a day for three days, then tapering down through two hundred fifty, one hundred twenty five, and sixty milligrams twice daily. For truly refractory ICANS, discuss alternative therapies such as anakinra, an anti IL one receptor agent, siltuximab, an anti IL six agent, or intrathecal or systemic chemotherapy.

keypoints: Grade two and up triggers ICU notification and neurology consult
